https://www.politico.eu/feed/.lastBody:
POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Tue, 20 Oct 2026 21:33:44 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-worries-donald-trump-prefers-vladimir-putin-volodymyr-zelenskyy-ukraine-war/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 20 Oct 2026 21:32:24 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9194807 In a throwaway comment this week, Donald Trump made clear that he does not regard the war in Ukraine as a conflict with fault on both sides. “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine,” the U.S. president said. “They have not been doing that much.”

To residents of Kyiv — who have endured weeks of intensifying bombardment — and Ukraine’s allies across Europe, the remark confirmed a growing impression that the U.S. is taking Russia leader Vladimir Putin’s side in the war.

“American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years,” the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday. The reason Ukraine hasn’t “surrendered on Putin’s terms” so far is because Europe has been providing so much support, she added. 

As they scratch their heads for explanations for Trump’s latest turn against Ukraine, some European officials and diplomats think it comes down to the president’s personal preferences, as much as his country’s political aims.

“I do think it’s a personal thing,” said former British Cabinet minister David Lidington, now distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a leading security think tank in London. “Trump is self-centered — his personal predilections for dictators and autocrats, his desire to give opportunities to U.S. businesses … are very important parts of his motivation.”

In private, EU officials agree. “Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. He just doesn’t like him,” said one government official who has observed both men closely. “That makes it harder to get the U.S. to help on peace. Everything is a rational business deal with Trump, until it’s not.” 

A diplomat from an EU country — granted anonymity, like others in this report, to discuss sensitive matters — said the inconsistent Trump could change his mind again and reverse recent moves against Ukraine. The U.S. president has chopped and changed on many issues, “except one thing,” the diplomat said. “He seems to be supportive of the Russians.”

“He’s been critical of Ukraine, the EU, NATO, but hardly ever said anything critical about Putin. It is striking. We have to deal with an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else,” the diplomat said.

The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mounting losses

For Ukraine and its European allies, the idea that nothing can or will change Trump’s feelings about Zelenskyy is a bleak one. After four-and-a-half years of war, Kyiv is running low on funding, air defenses and — amid swelling support for Europe’s populist right — facing a potential loss of political support in the months ahead. 

Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff met the Ukrainian president and the leaders of Norway and Finland for talks in Oslo on Tuesday, and will head to St. Petersburg to discuss peace proposals with the Russian leadership on Wednesday as the White House pushes hard for a ceasefire. One option Putin will be offered is a three-way leaders’ summit with Trump and Zelenskyy.

Previous efforts to get the Russian president to attend such a meeting have failed, however, and EU diplomats do not believe Putin is showing any genuine desire for a ceasefire. That is partly what makes Trump’s hostility toward Zelenskyy so problematic.

“There is a clear consensus across Europe that Putin does not want peace,” a second EU diplomat said. “He will need to be forced into peace.”

But instead of making demands of Putin, Trump has ratcheted up his pressure on Zelenskyy, even amid escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities this month. Ukraine’s leader is feeling the strain, as he told his EU counterparts in private meetings in Brussels last week, according to the first diplomat.

In a succession of highly critical comments in recent days, Trump has said Zelenskyy “doesn’t care” and “doesn’t want to end this war;” and should be replaced as leader or as Ukraine’s negotiator. “President Putin would like to see a settlement,” Trump said. “President Zelenskyy could have solved this war, or he could have made a deal, many times.” 

The Oval Office beating

Trump’s animosity may date back to an incident during his first term in 2019, when he urged the Ukrainian leader to help with an investigation into Joe Biden, who eventually defeated Trump in the following presidential election, Lidington said. A succession of hostile encounters in the years since — including in the Oval Office in February 2025 — have reinforced the impression, he said. 

“It was clear that in the infamous meeting in the White House that Trump and [Vice President JD] Vance had planned that public beating-up of Zelenskyy and it struck me then that there was a strong personal element to this,” said Lidington.

“I think there’s another element, which is that if you look at the people Trump tries to court, it tends to be autocratic strongman — and it is ‘man’ — leaders,” Lidington said.

He recalled attending a dinner with world leaders in 2018 to mark the centenary of the end of World War I in Paris. French President Emmanuel Macron and the German chancellor at the time, Angela Merkel, were playing joint hosts “at the top table,” but Trump was not interested in making small talk with either of them, Lidington said.

“It was pretty obvious from the body language that Trump was impatient with them and one of the people he really wanted to talk to was [Turkish leader Recep Tayyip] Erdoğan and other people who were a bit more in that strongman image that he likes to portray himself,” he observed.

‘Strange stories’

A senior official from a European country familiar with the Ukraine talks said Trump’s motives were partly political, partly about calculating what would be profitable and partly about personalities.

“They are currently in an election cycle and need someone to blame for rising prices,” the official said. “In general, Trump tends to like various types of people and leaders. He actually has a fondness for successful and cheerful people.”

In recent days, Zelenskyy has warned his country is suffering more civilian casualties because the U.S. has cut back on support, including Starlink and Starshield services that help Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks and plan operations. “We still have no explanation for this, just different strange stories,” Zelenskyy told U.S. congressmen on Monday.  

This month, the advanced warnings of incoming Russian missile attacks from U.S. partners have failed to come through as normal. Ukraine is also running low on Patriot missile interceptors, he said. 

The Pentagon has not issued an official comment on the Ukrainian complaints. The U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said 328 civilians were killed and more than 2,000 wounded across Ukraine last month, an 85% increase compared to September 2025. The U.N. said that the first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in Ukraine in years, driven by increased missile and drone strikes.

The first EU diplomat quoted above said many European governments were irritated that Trump had cut them out of his conversations with Putin so far. “There is probably much more dialogue between the Americans and the Russians than we might know,” the diplomat said. 

Tuesday’s meeting with Witkoff in Norway raised the possibility that direct engagement with Putin might be back on the cards, for Zelenskyy at least. 

“Today was a good day for peace,” Finland’s President Alexander Stubb said after attending the talks in Oslo. “On a substantive and technical level we have actually made a lot of progress under the radar in the past week or so and now I feel that the process is back on track,” Stubb said.

The process is now going in the right direction again, he added. “Hopefully, we don’t do any backtracking.”

]]> en Poland’s government votes to ease abortion laws in challenge to conservative president https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-parliament-eases-abortion-laws-ichallenge-conservative-president/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 20 Oct 2026 20:25:31 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9194630 WARSAW — Poland’s lower chamber of parliament approved two bills that would loosen the country’s strict abortion restrictions Tuesday evening, marking a breakthrough for Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s coalition nearly three years after it took power, promising to restore reproductive rights.

The measures, which are likely to be vetoed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, would end criminal penalties for helping a woman obtain an abortion and re-legalize terminations involving severe fetal abnormalities, undoing one of the crucial elements of Poland’s near-total abortion ban.

“The state trusts women. A woman who terminates her own pregnancy is already exempt from criminal punishment. It’s time to stop punishing everyone who loves us, worries about us and respects our choices,” Katarzyna Kotula, Poland’s government equality commissioner and a lawmaker from the Left, said on X.

Still, neither bill would allow abortion on request up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, as Tusk’s Civic Coalition promised during the 2023 election campaign. The multi-party coalition includes many conservatives and lacks agreement on the liberalization going this far.

Both bills now move from the lower chamber, or the Sejm, to the Senate, where they seem poised to pass, but their eventual fate remains uncertain. President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party, said before his election in 2025 that he would not sign legislation easing abortion rules.

“By refusing to sign [the abortion] legislation, the president is hurting people,” Włodzimierz Czarzasty, speaker of the Sejm, said Tuesday before the votes. “If he wants to hurt women, he will hurt them. I think women will see that and hear that.”

Tusk’s coalition government will likely keep turning up the heat on the president and PiS if Nawrocki blocks the liberalization, as he has said he would.

Overriding a presidential veto requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm that the Tusk-led coalition doesn’t have. The proposals that passed Tuesday lingered in a parliamentary committee for two years before surfacing, spurred by the campaign heating up 12 months before the next general election, slated for late 2027.

Overturning restrictions

At the parliamentary level, ending criminal penalties for helping women with abortion passed with 217 votes in favor, 213 against and three abstentions. The other bill won a slightly clearer majority of 233 for, 203 against and a single abstention.

The first bill would decriminalize assisting or encouraging an abortion performed outside legally permitted grounds, an offense which currently carries sentences of up to three years in prison. It would also protect doctors, nurses and midwives from prosecution when they terminate a pregnancy because of a threat to the woman’s life or health or strong indications of a serious, irreversible fetal condition.

The second bill would restore the right to terminate a pregnancy when doctors identify a severe and irreversible fetal abnormality or an incurable illness threatening the fetus’s viability. It would also set deadlines for hospitals to provide lawful abortions and require written explanations for refusals.

Women’s rights organizations were skeptical about the bills being a breakthrough, saying the reforms fall far short of granting Polish women the access to abortion available in most of the EU, where pregnancies can generally be terminated on request during the first trimester. 

“What does this mean for women who need abortions now? Nothing, because none of these projects would help them,” Legalna Aborcja (Legal Abortion) NGO said on X.

Education Minister Barbara Nowacka, acknowledging the incremental nature of the change, said she believed women should be able to decide, unconditionally, whether and how many children they have.

“But I voted for it and will always vote for every change, even the smallest one, that brings Polish women closer to full rights over their own lives.”

Poland does permit abortion where pregnancy threatens a woman’s health or life or results from a criminal act, including rape or incest. In October 2020, the Constitutional Tribunal, dominated by judges appointed under the PiS government, struck down the additional ground for serious fetal abnormalities, which one of the bills passed tonight restores.

The ruling, effective from January 2021, prompted huge street protests and dealt a lasting blow to PiS’ standing in the polls, contributing to the party’s eventual loss of power in the 2023 election.

Reversing the restrictions became a defining issue for Tusk’s pro-European camp ahead of the October 2023 election. But the governing agreement with the more conservative Polish People’s Party (PSL) and Poland 2050 prevented that. Some PSL and Poland 2050 lawmakers voted against the two bills tonight.

In July 2024, the Sejm rejected an attempt to decriminalize assistance with abortion by 218 votes to 215, after most PSL lawmakers joined the right-wing opposition in voting against it.

Nor was there much change in voting intentions toward far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whom the government has repeatedly blamed for stoking the violence. Mélenchon and his allies have repeatedly and forcefully denied the accusation.

The poll was conducted online from 8 p.m. Saturday — after rioting and looting had begun — until Monday.

Le Pen remains well ahead of the pack with 34% to 38% of the vote in the various scenarios tested. After localized curfews were established throughout the country Monday, Lecornu said it would be up to local and regional authorities to renew them Tuesday night.

]]> en 5 things the EU wants to change about its Arctic policy https://www.politico.eu/article/5-things-the-eu-wants-to-change-about-its-arctic-policy/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 20 Oct 2026 16:47:42 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9191453 BRUSSELS — The European Union is beefing up its presence in the Arctic to catch up with neighboring powers carving new trade lanes and drilling for resources under the melting ice.

On Tuesday, the EU unveiled a new plan called Northern Neighborhood. It’s meant to prepare for rising military and commercial activity in the north driven by climate change, and calls for new transport, research and security infrastructure in the region.

“The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding. And it’s not someone else’s frontier. It’s part of the European Union,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen declared as she unveiled the strategy.

She pointed to Russia’s expanding military footprint and the race for emerging shipping routes and critical resources as forces reshaping Europe’s security and economic future.

Climate change is dramatically affecting the Arctic. Planet-warming emissions are making the ice melt faster, disrupting the region’s fragile ecosystems. But where the ice is disappearing, countries like China, Russia and even Canada see an opportunity.

The EU is now scrambling to update its existing policies on the Arctic — once largely focused on environmental protection — to give more importance to security, shipping and extracting resources.

The strategy calls for a rebranding of the EU’s existing partnerships with Norway, Iceland, Canada and the U.K., backed by regular summits to set joint priorities and launch projects.

Here are five things Brussels wants to change about its Arctic policy.

1. Defense and security 

The strategy warns that Russia is rebuilding its military presence in the Arctic and that China has growing strategic ambitions in the region.

The EU plans to set up a pilot research project using satellite and maritime observation in 2027 and share ship-tracking data to help identify Russian shadow fleet vessels.

In the longer term, it wants EU countries to lead on a maritime security hub to pool intelligence on threats ranging from undersea cable sabotage to illegal fishing. It also calls for setting up an Arctic Cable Hub alongside NATO to monitor and protect subsea cables in the North Atlantic and the Arctic. The strategy lacks any information on funding for these projects, however.

Finnish MEP Mika Aaltola of the European People’s Party said the new focus on the Arctic is long overdue.

“Europe hasn’t been thinking about [the Arctic] enough,” Aaltola said. “Because of the ice melting and climate change, it’s becoming kind of the next great game. And if that happens, then what are the European positions when it comes to Russia, China and also the United States?”

2. Access to energy resources

The new policy sticks with EU promises not to drill for fossil fuels in the Arctic.

“The EU remains committed to ensuring that oil, coal and gas stay in the ground, including in Arctic regions,” it reads. Instead, Brussels promises to develop renewable energy projects in the region but drops an old commitment to convince the rest of the world to follow its lead. 

“It is good that the Commission maintains its opposition to oil and gas drilling in the Arctic,” said Delara Burkhardt, a Socialist MEP, but not pressing for a global ban “weakens the EU’s ability to push for stronger international protection and leaves the door open for other countries to exploit one of the world’s most fragile ecosystems.”

The EU’s former Arctic policy — drafted in 2021 — committed the bloc to pursuing an international moratorium on Arctic oil and gas extraction. 

Norway — which supplies a lot of energy to the EU — has made it clear it would still drill in the Arctic regardless of the bloc’s position.

3. Critical raw materials 

The EU is under pressure to secure new supplies of critical raw materials to reduce its dependency on China.

The new strategy says it will continue working with Canada, Greenland, Norway and the United States to develop critical raw materials projects in the region, but insists it will do so while following the “highest social, environmental and governance standards,” and work to the “benefit of local communities in respect of Indigenous Peoples’ rights.” 

Brussels has already labeled several critical raw materials projects, including the Sokli project in Finland and the Per Geijer rare earth deposit in northern Sweden, as “strategic” under EU law, which means they could benefit from faster permitting procedures.  

But some of these projects face serious local resistance from local and indigenous communities, who say the mining plans threaten reindeer herding and protected ecological sites. 

4. New trade routes

Melting ice is opening up new shipping routes in the far north, and the EU is worried that it could be sidelined from the region. But the strategy offers little on that front; its only action is a study on new shipping lanes.

The number of vessels operating in the area covered by the Polar Code — international regulations covering shipping in the Arctic and Antarctic — rose by 40% between 2013 and 2025, while the total distance sailed nearly doubled, said Michael Kingston, a special adviser on polar issues to the Arctic Council on marine protection.

Recent transits by Chinese and South Korean container ships using the Northern Sea Route running along Russia’s Arctic coast show the appeal of a route that is about 20 days faster than conventional routes, he added. 

“Russia builds the infrastructure, China facilitates and funds some of it,” Aaltola said, calling it part of a “grand bargain” between the two.

He complained that the EU is left on the sidelines. “When it comes to the Arctic, there is a vacuum of interest, and there’s also a vacuum of resources and institutions participating.” 

The route is still mostly seasonal for Russian oil and gas tankers, said Ksenia Vakhrusheva, project manager and Arctic project adviser at the environmental group Bellona. Ice, unpredictable weather, increased insurance costs and Moscow’s control over the route make it unlikely to become a mainstream commercial corridor anytime soon, she added.  

Europe also has leverage as the final customer for Chinese shipments, Vakhrusheva said.

“If the EU sends a strong message to China that they do not want goods shipped via NSR, China won’t use this route for transit,” she said. “For NSR to become a valid transit route you need two sides,” she said, “a seller on one side and a buyer on the other.” 

5. Environmental protection 

The strategy is light on measures to shield the Arctic from the impact of global warming. However, it does warn that increased shipping in an “inherently harsh and poorly charted environment” raises the risk of “catastrophic accidents, severe marine pollution” and hybrid interference.  

“Increased shipping in the Arctic both exploits this vulnerability and exacerbates it,” said Dave Walsh, an adviser at the Clean Arctic Alliance NGO, citing carbon emissions, wastewater discharge and noise as some of the impacts of more traffic.

Safety and the environment have not been a priority for Moscow, said Vakhrusheva, and a shortage of high ice-class ships combined with the need to sell oil and gas “to whoever is ready to buy it” raises the risks. 

Protections such as a ban on heavy fuel oil are still negotiated at the International Maritime Organization, where the EU is a key player, she said, adding that such measures will push up the cost of Arctic shipping. 

The strategy says Brussels will push at the IMO to turn measures to limit black carbon — soot emitted by ships that falls on snow and ice and accelerates melting — from voluntary guidelines into binding rules.

It also calls for expanding the definition of Arctic waters to everything north of 60 degrees latitude, replacing the current boundary, which excludes much of the waters around Iceland and Norway from special Arctic shipping rules.

It also promises to keep pressing for compliance with the Polar Code through tools such as an IMO regulation that involves national maritime authorities inspecting foreign-flagged ships in Arctic ports to verify compliance with international safety, environmental and crew-qualification standards. 

The document includes non-binding commitments on biodiversity loss and plans to boost ocean and Arctic research programs. It also promises to launch an “initiative to promote local public and private investment in the Arctic around blue economy sectors.” 

Jakob Weizman contributed reporting.

“I am grateful for his willingness to help and his clear position. First, it’s about interceptors against ballistic missiles, which are needed to protect lives. Second, it’s about early warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks, which is vital. Third, it’s about the situation around Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored,” he said in a social media post.

The growing frictions with the U.S. come as President Donald Trump ramps up pressure on Kyiv to stop hitting Russian oil refineries and to reach a peace deal with Moscow.

“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine … They have not been doing that much,” Trump told reporters on Monday.

Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway on Tuesday for a new round of talks on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.

U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said that 328 civilians were killed and more than 2,000 wounded across Ukraine last month, an 85% increase from September 2025. The U.N. said that the first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in years, driven by intensified missile and drone strikes.

This story has been updated. Seb Starcevic contributed reporting.

It’s over. https://euobserver.com/243724/the-us-is-no-longer-an-ally-its-over/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243724 Even an eventual change of American leadership doesn't mean the US's bizarre glorification of violence goes away. It is a persistent stain, constantly eroding away at the values of an open and free society. Both are worth defending here in Europe. The US has chosen its own path. Let it walk it alone.]]> Years ago I was flipping through the ads of a ‘Black Friday’ sale from a large US retailer, while visiting a relative in North Carolina. Amid the pens and pencils was a child’s school bag with a large neon printed unicorn surrounded by lollipops and or hearts.

It was bullet proof.

I can’t recall what caliber of bullet it promised to stop. But the same paper had a semi-automatic Bushmaster rifle for sale at only $549.99 [€490], which normally retails at almost $1,000. I snapped a photo of it.

A few years earlier, a Bushmaster had been used to gun down 20 small children at Sandy Hook Elementary. Most of them were only six-years old.

A Benenlli 12-gauge tactical shotgun was also on sale. Last week, five-year-old Rhoam Summer and two others, aged 8 and 11 were shot dead at a school in Oregon by a 16-year old with a shotgun.

I mention this as someone who grew up in the United States and went to school there but can’t identify with a normalisation of violence splashed out as one-off specials and deals ahead of Christmas, a holiday that is cynically meant to celebrate peace and kindness.

]]> EU unlikely to send Black Sea naval mission to repel Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian grain ships, despite Kallas’ support https://euobserver.com/243857/eu-unlikely-to-send-black-sea-naval-mission-to-repel-russian-drone-attacks-on-ukrainian-grain-ships-despite-kallas-support/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 16:55:52 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243857 The EU's top diplomat has backed the idea of a Black Sea naval mission to protect grain ships from Russian drones - but this would require much more than Europe's existing Red Sea operation, while air policing might be more effective.]]> The EU’s top diplomat has backed the idea of a Black Sea naval mission to protect grain ships from Russian drones – but this would require much more than Brussels’ existing Red Sea operation, while air policing might be more effective.

“The EU should send a mission to the Black Sea,” said EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas in the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday (20 October).

“To protect merchant shipping, not to escalate, not to scare anyone, but to make sure that we will supply safely fuel, merchandise at normal prices, anything we need. This is how it should be,” she said.

Some “six attacks in 10 days by suspected Russian drones marks a dangerous and unacceptable escalation in the Black Sea,” Kallas added, with “rescuers
still searching for seven sailors missing after the drone attack on two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast”.

The Russian attacks were costing Ukraine €60m a day in lost exports of grain and fertiliser, Kallas also said.

And Russia had changed its tactics to start targeting people instead of cargo, said Sidharth Kaushal, from the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) defence think-tank in London.

“Before, they targeted ports, not civilians, or vessels at sea. They realised that threat to life is a much more effective deterrent to commercial shipping than threat to cargo,” he told EUobserver.

]]> MEPs push to use EU regional funds for affordable housing and climate‑proofing cities https://euobserver.com/243837/meps-push-to-use-eu-regional-funds-for-affordable-housing-and-climateproofing-cities/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 16:33:38 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243837 The European Parliament called on more spending to build affordable houses, using funds for regional development that currently comprise up to a third of the present EU budget.]]> The European Parliament has called for more spending to build affordable houses — using funds for regional development that currently make up a third of the EU budget.

Cohesion funds should be used to protect the ‘right to stay’ in rural areas or in small cities, a principle that the parliament wants to write into the new budget legislation.

Peripheral regions often face depopulation due to few job opportunities, according to a parliamentary non-binding report passed with 601 votes in favour, 20 against, and 36 abstentions on Tuesday (20 October).

Read more

The forgotten protests: empty shelves and blocked roads in southern Italy, ignored by the media, reveal neglect by Meloni and EU

MEPs are also calling for strong cohesion funds that would allow cities to better prepare for climate emergencies and provide a budget for additional investments in housing.

Cohesion funds, which account for a total of €48.03bn in the existing 2021-2027 EU budget, usually finance infrastructure projects, like bridges, roads, or railways in countries with a lower-than-average per capita gross national income.

The commission proposed significant cuts to reduce regional funds in the next multi-annual budget, set to cover 2028-34, but a group of 16 member states, often benefitting from the funding, opposed the reduction.

Read more

Frugal EU states seeking budget cuts are shooting their own regions in the foot

Regional development plays a key role in European integration since it is the “only instrument which can unite all of us,” and should not be reduced in the next EU budget, said Left Lithuanian MEP Vytenis Povilas Andriukaitis during a plenary debate on Monday (19 October).

Cohesion funds “could be the response to the radicalisation of Europe,” Fredis Beleris, a German centre-right MEP said.

For that to happen, cohesion funds must be accessible for small and medium-sized cities, who often struggle with formalities linked to EU funds, said Denis Nesci, Italian conservative MEP spearheading the file.

Small municipalities should be able to access cohesion funds “on an equal footing as bigger cities,” he said, echoing the dominant centre-right commission’s position and its aim to simplify regulations.

]]> MEPs open arms to UK rejoining EU to ‘correct’ Brexit mistake https://euobserver.com/243824/meps-open-arms-to-a-uk-rejoin-to-correct-brexit-mistake/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 16:10:38 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243824 Members of European Parliament from across the political spectrum are holding the door open for Britain to rejoin the union.]]> A diverse array of MEPs on Tuesday (20 October) expressed their enthusiasm for the UK ‘correcting the mistake’ of Brexit by rejoining the European Union 10 years after its people narrowly voted to leave.

“Trump, Xi and Putin might form a troika of iliberalism standing in defiance of the achievements of liberal democracy”, warned Barry Andrews, an Irish MEP for Renew, saying that the EU should not treat the United Kingdom “like any other third country”.

His party ally Sandro Gozi, an Italian MEP, added: “Every option must be on the table, from a special partnership to full EU membership.” 

The debate on EU-UK relations in the Strasbourg parliament came a month ahead of a highly-anticipated EU-UK summit in Brussels on 20 November. 

Read more

Burnham to prioritise trade and migration at UK-EU summit, after accusing Russia of meddling in Brexit referendum

Although the UK rejoining the bloc is still a distant prospect, it is back on the agenda because of new prime minister Andy Burnham.

Brexit had “done more harm than good”, Burnham told delegates at the Labour party conference in late September, adding that “we will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of the century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market.” 

Britain could “go all the way” back into the EU, added Burnham.

European parliament president Robert Metsola has given an open invitation for Burnham to address MEPs, her office told EUobserver, in another sign of goodwill.

The UK Treasury, meanwhile, is expected to publish a study in the coming days detailing the scale of the hit to the UK economy from leaving the bloc.

Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, who resigned in July primarily because of dismal opinion poll ratings, had promised a ‘reset’ of EU-UK relations when his government took power in July 2024. But apart from rhetoric, little has changed, though the UK now has access to the Erasmus+ student exchange programme.

Brexit is a “mistake that can be corrected by all of us” and admitting it is “a sign of strength”, said German Green MEP Terry Reintke.

New deals agreed should be “the floor and not the ceiling” of bilateral relations, said David McAllister, a German MEP for the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP).

On the right, Polish MEP for the European Conservatives and Reformists Jadwiga Wiśniewska also welcomed new talks with the UK, calling for them to be based on “concrete elements” like agriculture deals, defence and Erasmus+.

]]> EU vows to stop buying Arctic oil and gas, but drops ban from its new strategy https://euobserver.com/243804/eu-vows-to-stop-buying-arctic-oil-and-gas-but-drops-ban-from-its-new-strategy/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 14:40:39 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243804 EU officials vowed an end to Arctic oil and gas buying, as the European Commission presented its new Arctic strategy. But while the document commits to keeping Arctic oil and gas “in the ground,” it drops the call for an international ban.]]> The EU “will not drill and will not buy” Arctic oil and gas, EU officials said on Tuesday (20 October), as the European Commission presented its new Arctic strategy. 

“Our position on Arctic oil, gas and coal has not changed,” a senior EU official told reporters. “It’s fairly simple. We will not drill in the Arctic, and we will not buy hydrocarbons from the Arctic.”

The strategy follows months of heavy lobbying by Norway’s prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre and his cabinet. 

Oslo used the energy supply disruption caused by the Iran war to push the EU to drop its 2021 support for a moratorium on oil and gas drilling in the Arctic, insisting that it was crucial for future energy security. 

But EU officials made clear on Tuesday they did not buy that argument. “We do not need Arctic resources to keep our energy supply secure,” the official said.

]]> Ukrainians evacuate soldier using heavy air drone after he spent 500 days at the front, in another first-ever in the war (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,699) https://euobserver.com/243780/ukrainians-evacuate-soldier-using-heavy-air-drone-after-he-spent-500-days-at-the-front-in-another-first-ever-in-the-war-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1699/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 13:41:08 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243780 While US secretary of state Marco Rubio publicly echoes Vladimir Putin’s inflated claims about Russian gains in Donetsk, Ukrainian crews on the ground are using scarce drones to snatch back their own wounded from territory Moscow says it controls.]]>
  • For the first time, Ukrainians rescued a wounded soldier by air.
  • He spent 500 days at the front, during which he had to amputate his own legs.
  • How the operation unfolded and what Ukrainians had to do to distract Russian drones.
  • Rubio repeats Putin’s claims about occupied territory in the Donetsk region.
  • Videos of the day: the first capture of a Russian tank this year; a swarm of Ukrainian drones.

    • The information in this text is a summary of events on Monday (19 October). The situation may have changed since then.

    Hardly a week passes without some new development being reported on the frontline of Russia’s war in Ukraine. This time, Ukrainians demonstrated something truly unique. For the first time, they succeeded in evacuating a wounded soldier using a heavy rotary-wing aerial drone.

    The story was published by the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade and reported by a journalist from the Oboronka website, who spoke to both the operators and the wounded soldier. The evacuation took place near Kupiansk in the Kharkiv region, on the left, or eastern, bank of the Oskil river.

    Infantryman Kostiantyn ‘Magura’ Vlasenko of the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade was tasked, together with a comrade, with heading into the grey zone in early June 2025.

    Initially, they hid in one place, but when their position was flooded, they had to leave the building and take shelter elsewhere. Returning was impossible because of the dangerous situation. His comrade later died.

    In February this year, Magura was also wounded by a Russian drone. Munitions dropped from the drone injured both his legs. According to Oboronka, he had to amputate his own lower limbs in order to survive.

    The website did not give details of how he managed to do this. Similar cases have, however, occurred in the past.

    In 2018, for instance, during an exercise in Slovakia, an American soldier was trapped beneath a tank. He amputated his own leg to save a fellow soldier, for which he was named Soldier of the Year in 2021.

    In Magura’s case, this meant he was left immobile, and it was clear that he would not return from the front by himself.

    Ukrainian units considered how to help him. The situation was extremely difficult in this respect.

    ]]>         Europe’s €800bn defence borrowing hides a reality of every country buying on its own https://euobserver.com/243439/europes-e800bn-defence-spending-splurge-yet-its-a-sellers-market-if-the-eu-barely-borrows-together-and-buys-alone/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 11:06:56 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243439 In defence, the bigger the order, the longer the production line and the lower the cost of each unit. That is a big reason why Europe has long bought American, for price as much as for technology. Europe could match it by buying together and sharing out the work along the value chain.]]> Europe is supposed to be financing its defence together. It barely is.

    Of the €800bn announced under ReArm Europe in March 2025, €650bn is not common money. It is an estimate of the extra room governments get under the national escape clause to spend up to 1.5 percent of GDP more on defence for four years.

    Each country still pays for that spending itself.

    The room is also temporary: EU Commission simulations suggest that maintaining higher defence spending after 2028 could require additional annual fiscal adjustment of 0.25 to 0.4 percentage points of GDP from 2029.

    The other €150bn is SAFE, and it is loans, not grants.

    The EU borrows and lends the money on, and each country repays its share. Grants are small: €1.5bn from the European Defence Industry Programme for 2025-2027, plus the European Defence Fund for joint research.

    Not every country has used these tools, as Table 1 shows. The Netherlands and Sweden have used neither. Like Germany, which has taken only the clause, they can borrow at least as cheaply as the EU, so SAFE gets them nothing.

    France has taken SAFE but not the clause, to protect the credibility of its budget plans.

    Table 1. Who uses SAFE and the national escape clause

    Source: Council of the EU, European Commission. Data as of 17 October 2026. * Hungary: allocated €16.2bn, now requesting €5.4bn; still pending. ** Italy: the Commission backed its request on 8 October 2026; the Council has yet to decide.

    Where SAFE does matter is on the eastern flank. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia can borrow the equivalent of five to eight percent of their GDP, and Poland almost five percent.

    Graph 1. SAFE loans as a share of GDP, by country (%)

    Source: Council of the EU, European Commission, Eurostat. SAFE loans only, as a share of 2025 GDP. Amounts approved by the Council, except Italy and Hungary (* revised requests of €8bn and €5.4bn, September 2026). Data as of 17 October 2026.

    That leaves private money.

    The European Investment Bank and the European Investment Fund are trying to bring in private investors, partly by removing the reputational stigma of financing defence.

    But defence is almost a monopsony: the state is nearly the only buyer. Without a clear flow of public orders, private investment will be hard to come by.

    So Europe barely borrows together. And it buys alone.

    ]]>         MEPs resist 17% cut to EU foreign aid, instead seek €25bn top‑up https://euobserver.com/243706/meps-resist-17-cut-to-eu-foreign-aid-instead-seek-e25bn-topup/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 11:05:55 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243706 MEPs insist that they won't allow EU governments to dictate the terms of the bloc's next seven-year budget, and have called for an extra €25bn in spending on the EU's foreign policy agenda.]]> MEPs have put themselves on a collision course with EU governments by rejecting plans for a 17-percent cut in foreign spending – instead demanding additional spending worth €25bn. 

    Earlier this month, the Irish government, which holds the six-month rotating EU council presidency, proposed that €38bn of cuts be made from the ‘Global Europe’ heading, which covers foreign aid, as part of an overall package of €141bn of cuts to the seven-year EU budget, known as the multi-annual financial framework (MFF). 

    But in a vote on Monday evening (19 October), the European Parliament’s development committee instead backed a dedicated minimum budget of €25bn for humanitarian aid, as well as dedicated budget lines for a Gaza reconstruction fund and for candidate countries. Put together, that would mean a €25bn increase on the EU Commission’s original budget of €200bn for the Global Europe heading. 

    The position agreed by MEPs, by a 61-to-34 vote margin, will eventually form the basis of negotiations between MEPs and ministers when EU governments agree their position on the budget.

    ]]>         PM Babiš blames press for ANO election loss, renews calls to abolish license fees for Czech public media https://euobserver.com/243606/pm-babis-blames-press-for-ano-election-loss-renews-calls-to-abolish-license-fees-for-czech-public-media/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 10:17:13 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243606 Andrej Babiš vows no policy retreat after ANO's election flop. With the opposition gaining ground in a weekend senate vote in Czech Republic, the prime minister has moved to scrap public media license fees.]]> First published in Respekt.

    Before the Czech election results were announced, a WhatsApp group used to alert journalists of prime minister Andrej Babiš’s public appearances went quiet. Reporters asking if and when the ANO leader would make a statement, were met with the same answer from party officials: ‘we don’t know’.

    Anticipating poor run-off results for the Senate (upper house), the party had not planned any major press events. Instead, Babiš arrived at his local polling venue – a sports hall – on Saturday (17 October) afternoon, to concede defeat.

    In the 2024 Senate elections, ANO had gained eight seats, but this year lost the one seat it was defending.

    The opposition party of Mayors and Independents (STAN) performed best, winning ten of the 14 seats it contested.

    Having climbed in the polls in recent months, the party now believes it could lead the opposition into the next general election against the ANO-led government.

    Read more

    Babiš’s ‘blind trust’ under fire: EU says Czech PM still benefits from Agrofert profits

    Pro-Babiš candidates defeated

    Babiš and his supporters could hardly have asked for a better starting position this year: ANO was defending just one mandate, and its senate group had 15 seats before the vote.

    Babiš said his party had an exceptional chance to break the opposition parties’ long-standing majority to take control of the upper house.

    But that goal was quickly out of reach. ANO would have needed to win in all 27 districts, but fielded candidates in only 24 of them.

    When only 13 ANO candidates advanced to the second round, the prime minister’s appearances in the days before the vote suggested he no longer believed ANO could win. “The second round will see the same old story – everyone will join forces against us,” Babiš said.

    ANO also fielded low-profile or inexperienced candidates, while STAN party leader Vít Rakušan personally travelled to support candidates throughout the campaign.

    Read more

    Denmark lashes out again at Sánchez over Spain’s migration regularisation, but EU summit avoids linking migration to crime

    Analysts have attributed ANO’s poor performance to its poor choice of candidates. They point, among others, to Sandra Tsoukernik, the wife of a controversial businessman in the gambling industry who ran in the Tachov and Cheb district against incumbent senator Miroslav Plevný, a professor of economics.

    Tsoukernik diligently toured her district, but unlike Plevný she did not speak about her programme at meetings with voters — or anywhere else.

    Although Tsoukernik managed to fill town squares by hiring the pianist Michal David, this was widely viewed as a publicity stunt.

    ]]>         Generation Z in France, Spain and Albania is trapped: study hard, stay poor, live with your parents.     One concession in exchange for the other. French president Emmanuel Macron and German chancellor Friedrich Merz have now sealed the deal.

    Both can claim victory at home, and both say they want the same thing: to strengthen Europe’s auto industry against Chinese competition. 

    But the trade-off undermines that very goal. It rightly pushes for more European production, but pays for it with less ambition for electric vehicles.

    For Europe’s automakers to compete, two things need to happen: More of the value generated by car manufacturing must stay in Europe, and the transition to electric vehicles must remain on track. Trading one for the other weakens both. 

    Value creation is already moving elsewhere 

    On one point, France is right: a growing EV market alone won’t protect European jobs. Many of the most important components in electric cars already come from China, especially batteries.

    Meanwhile, Chinese automakers are building factories in Hungary and Spain, securing direct access to the European market. 

    The risk is clear: cars assembled in Europe from imported components qualify as European products, benefit from purchase incentives and win public contracts.

    Final assembly stays in Europe, but much of the economic value is created elsewhere. European auto suppliers have already cut more than 100,000 jobs in two years, and the European Commission warns that up to 600,000 more could disappear over the next five to 10 years. 

    Read more

    That’s where the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act comes in. It would link public spending on subsidies, purchase incentives and government procurement to production in Europe.

    This isn’t just about shutting out foreign competition. It steers demand to where it strengthens Europe’s industrial base.

    To work, the rules must target the components that will shape the industry’s future: battery cells, software, electric drivetrains and power electronics.

    “Made in Europe” can’t simply mean attaching the wheels here. 

    That doesn’t mean every nut and bolt must come from the EU.  The auto industry relies on global supply chains and trusted trading partners.

    But a law riddled with exemptions would be little better than no law at all: It would create more red tape without bringing a single new factory to Europe. 

    Factories need customers 

    Even the best industrial policy will fail without buyers. A battery factory can only make money if it produces enough batteries. Yet Europe’s battery plants are running well below capacity because they don’t have enough orders. Every battery that goes unproduced drives up the cost of those that are made.     This deal is not yet law. A better deal would be simple: Europe should pursue electric vehicles with the same determination as China while making sure the jobs, factories and economic benefits stay in Europe.

    At international level, the EU also played a decisive role in the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which was agreed in December 2022 at COP15 of the Convention on Biological Diversity. The framework established a global roadmap to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. 

    Next week (19-30 October), Yerevan will host COP17 of the Convention, where the first global review of progress since the adoption of the Framework will take place. It will be an important opportunity to determine whether the commitments made are being translated into concrete action and results on the ground. 

    As co-chair of the European Parliament delegation attending the conference, I will defend a united European position that is consistent with our historic leadership and responds to the urgency of the challenge.

    The European Commission, which formally negotiates on behalf of the Union on the basis of the position agreed with the member states, must promote decisions that accelerate implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework during the remaining years to 2030. 

    Honest appraisal? A mixed picture

    This global review must be accompanied by an honest assessment of our own performance. Europe should arrive in Yerevan acknowledging both the progress it has made and the work that remains.

    The commission’s latest report on the implementation of the framework presents a mixed picture.

    Of the 45 targets established for the EU, only two have been achieved and 16 are on track, while progress remains too slow on another 25 and two cannot yet be assessed. 

    There are positive signs in the EU. Protected areas have expanded, organic farming has increased and a greater proportion of fish stocks is being managed sustainably.

    However, the overall situation of many habitats and species remains worrying, while farmland birds and grassland butterflies, among others, continue to decline. 

    The main problem is not a lack of legislation, as Europe already has many of the instruments it needs. The challenge is to implement them properly and turn them into visible improvements on the ground, which requires public authorities with sufficient capacity, reliable data, clear plans and stable funding. 

    The Nature Restoration Regulation is a good example.

    Restoring wetlands, rivers, forests, soils and marine ecosystems will not only help biodiversity recover, but will also retain water, reduce flood damage, protect soils and make our territories more resilient to droughts, heatwaves and wildfires. 

    Missed deadlines

    However, the regulation will only deliver results if member states meet their obligations.

    The deadline for submitting draft national restoration plans was 1 September, yet only nine countries have done so.

    This delay not only slows implementation, but also makes it harder to calculate the cost of restoring nature and the resources that will be required. 

    Read more

    ‘Cementing over our own future’: Europe’s nature loss is 600 football pitches daily

    The commission was expected to present an assessment of restoration funding needs and gaps in August 2025, but we are still waiting for a complete analysis.

    The commission argues that it needs the national plans to calculate these costs. Yet negotiations on the 2028-2034 financial framework are moving forward while many plans remain outstanding and we still lack a full estimate of the resources needed to implement one of our most important environmental laws. 

    This situation reflects one of the main challenges facing COP17.

    Adopting targets is no longer enough. We must also agree on how they will be implemented, how progress will be measured and how action will be financed.

    Five EU priorities in Yerevan

    In this context, I believe that the European position should focus on five priorities. We must mobilise more resources for biodiversity, consolidate the Cali Fund, make progress in eliminating harmful subsidies, assess progress through concrete results and strengthen the role of nature in climate adaptation. 

    Finance will be one of the central issues in Yerevan, as the Global Biodiversity Framework calls for the mobilisation of at least $200bn [€178bn] a year from all sources by 2030. Public investment must remain the foundation of this effort, but private capital will also be needed.

    With this aim, the commission presented its roadmap for nature credits in July 2025 and is now developing the methodologies, certification systems, oversight arrangements and pilot projects needed for their deployment.

    These instruments could help finance conservation and restoration, but they will only be useful if they are governed by rigorous rules and deliver real, verifiable and additional benefits for biodiversity. They must never replace public funding or be used to justify damage to nature in one place in exchange for financing action elsewhere. 

    COP17 must also consolidate the Cali Fund, which was created so that companies benefiting from the use of digital information on genetic resources contribute to biodiversity conservation. The agreement reached at COP16 was an important step, but we now need real contributions and a fair distribution of resources, including for Indigenous Peoples and local communities. 

    Another priority must be to eliminate incentives and subsidies that harm biodiversity. It makes no sense to call for new resources to protect nature while public budgets continue to support activities that destroy it.

    The European Union should therefore examine its own policies honestly, particularly in areas such as agriculture, fisheries, energy and infrastructure, and establish a timetable for progressively phasing out and ultimately eliminating this harmful support. 

    The global review must also measure concrete results. Success cannot be assessed simply by counting strategies or setting targets. We need to know whether ecosystems are recovering, whether species are in better condition, whether protected areas are being managed effectively and whether funding is actually reaching action on the ground. 

    We must also strengthen the connection between biodiversity and climate adaptation. The droughts, floods, heatwaves and wildfires affecting Europe show that protecting and restoring nature is not a secondary concern. Healthy ecosystems are among our best defences against the effects of climate change and represent a direct investment in our security, agriculture and economy. 

    All these priorities lead us inevitably to the European budget, because political commitments are only credible when they are backed by sufficient resources.

    The budget?

    There is currently a clear contradiction between the leadership that the European Union wishes to maintain on biodiversity and the place given to it in the proposal for the 2028-2034 financial framework.

    Although the commission proposes that 35 percent of the next budget should contribute jointly to climate and environmental objectives, it removes the specific 10 percent target for biodiversity included in the current budget and no longer presents LIFE as a standalone programme.

    By placing biodiversity within much broader objectives and funds, its financing becomes less visible and risks being pushed aside by priorities such as security, defence and competitiveness. 

    Parliament must defend sufficient and clearly identifiable resources for biodiversity and for the activities currently financed through LIFE.

    Simplification can make funding easier to access, but it must not reduce environmental ambition, transparency or democratic oversight. 

    This budget debate also affects our international credibility. Europe cannot ask other countries to increase their ambition and financial contributions while weakening budgetary support for biodiversity within the Union itself. Our leadership in Yerevan will depend not only on what we defend in the negotiations, but also on what we are able to implement and finance at home. 

    Europe has strong laws, valuable experience and the capacity to lead. We do not need to start again. We need to deliver what we have already agreed, provide the necessary resources and use COP17 to accelerate global action. 

    The global review cannot be limited to describing how far we remain from the 2030 targets. It must help us agree on how to close that gap during the four years that remain. I will travel to Yerevan with the European Parliament delegation determined to support that objective. 

    ]]>

]]> Après une escale à La Réunion l’année dernière, le Fundtruck a de nouveau posé ses valises dans l’océan Indien, en associant cette fois La Réunion et Mayotte au sein d’une même étape. Le 24 septembre, Maddyness a ainsi organisé une étape hybride depuis le siège de la BRED à Saint-Denis, permettant aux entrepreneuses et entrepreneurs des deux territoires de présenter leur projet dans les mêmes conditions que les candidats de l’Hexagone.

Une étape entre La Réunion et Mayotte

Huit startups réunionnaises et mahoraises étaient en lice pour décrocher leur place en finale. Comme à chaque étape du Fundtruck, les entrepreneurs disposaient de trois minutes pour pitcher leur projet, avant cinq minutes de questions face à un jury composé d’investisseurs et d’acteurs de l’écosystème.

Pour cette édition particulière, 16 membres du jury se sont mobilisés, sur place à La Réunion ou à distance, afin d’écouter et de challenger les différents projets. 

À l’issue des délibérations, c’est CapstonAI qui s’est imposée auprès du jury. Fondée par Greg Hanffou, la startup accompagne les entreprises pour améliorer leur visibilité dans les réponses générées par les principaux outils d’intelligence artificielle, comme ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude et Perplexity.

Faire rayonner les écosystèmes ultramarins

Cette étape a permis de mettre une nouvelle fois en lumière le dynamisme entrepreneurial de territoires encore éloignés des grands hubs de l’innovation métropolitains. 

L’étape 2026 a pu aussi compter sur le soutien de la BRED Banque Populaire, partenaire de cette escale, ainsi que de La French Tech La Réunion, Bpifrance, IVECO, Electra, CF Advisory et CF - Compagnie Fiduciaire, avec Manuel Biota.

CapstonAI rejoint désormais les autres lauréats de la saison et se prépare à représenter La Réunion et Mayotte lors de la Grande Finale du Fundtruck 2026. Celle-ci aura lieu le 26 novembre au siège de LCL.. La tournée, elle, se poursuit avec des nouvelles étapes en Île-de-France, en Belgique, puis à Bordeaux.

      <title>Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/20/ai-actors-val-kilmer-as-deep-as-the-grave-tilly-norwood</link>
      <description><p>As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner</p><p>‘Don’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.</p><p>Not just yet, judging by the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G0L8wTLaS8U">extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year</a>: it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/20/ai-actors-val-kilmer-as-deep-as-the-grave-tilly-norwood">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/oct/14/us-economy-affordability-midterm-elections-republicans-trump">Our reporters answer your questions on whether Trump’s economy will sink Republicans in the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>When partners consider finances, when is it ‘my’ money, and when it is ‘our’ money? <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 21 Oct 2026 00:44:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[State’s population surges by almost 800,000 in a decade]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/states-population-surges-by-almost-800000-in-a-decade/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/states-population-surges-by-almost-800000-in-a-decade/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 15:21:37 +0000The State’s population has risen by almost 800,000 in the last decade, with two-thirds of the increase coming from net inward migration.

Figures indicate that the Republic’s population grew by 786,000 or 16.6 per cent between 2016 and 2026 to stand at 5.5 million.

This was the third highest increase in the European Union behind Malta and Luxembourg. It compares to an overall EU population increase of less than 2 per cent.

The Central Statistics Office said the Republic’s population growth was driven by positive net migration and by a natural increase as a result of more births than deaths.

Net migration – the difference between the number of people moving to and from the State – totalled 511,000 since 2016, which accounted for 65 per cent of the overall increase in population here.

“Over the last 10 years, Ireland has consistently recorded positive net migration,” the CSO said.

“However, net migration in 2026 fell by 19.4 per cent (to 48,100) compared with the previous year. Net migration peaked at 79,300 in 2024,” it said.

The agency’s latest Measuring Ireland’s Progress report noted that over the last 10 years the natural increase in the population (births minus deaths) has almost halved, from 35,600 in 2016 to 18,800 in 2026.

During the period, the proportion of the population aged 45 and over rose from 37.1 per cent to 42.2 per cent, whereas the proportion aged under 45 fell from 62.9 per cent to 57.8 per cent.

In 2025, Ireland also had the highest young-age dependency ratio in the EU at 28.1 per cent. This ratio measures the number of children aged under 15 years as a proportion of the “working-age population” aged 15-64.

The State also had the second lowest old-age dependency ratio (the number of people aged 65 or over as a proportion of those aged 15-64) in the EU at 23.8 per cent.

With households in the grip of another inflationary surge, the CSO’s report also noted Ireland had the second-highest price level for consumer goods and services in the EU in 2025 at 36.2 per cent above the EU average, while Denmark had the highest at 39.7 per cent above average.

The figures also indicated that the State’s national debt has fallen to its lowest level since the banking crisis began in 2008.

Total debt fell to just under €210 billion last year, equating to 63 per cent of modified gross national income (GNI*), the agency’s bespoke measure of national income here.

In the wake of the banking bailouts post-2008, Ireland’s debt as a percentage of GNI* soared to 166 per cent.

The State’s improved debt picture since then stands in stark contrast to the trend internationally, with debt crises engulfing several countries, most notably France, the United States and the United Kingdom.

France’s debt – at €3.6 trillion – is currently 120 per cent of the country’s income. The worsening trajectory of its annual fiscal deficit has triggered a surge in French bond yields, hiking up the annual cost of servicing its debt.

Ireland’s debt-to-GDP ratio has been helped more by the rise in national income rather than a reduction in the debt itself.

The State’s GDP has doubled to €602.4 billion since 2015 on the back of huge multinational-led investment.

As a percentage of GDP, Ireland’s debt was 32.9 per cent last year, the fifth-lowest government debt-to-GDP ratio in the EU.

However, it still equated to €37,988 for every person in the State, which is large by international standards.

CSO’s figures also indicated that Ireland recorded the highest annual GDP growth rate within the EU, at 8 per cent.

This represented a reversal from 2023, when Ireland experienced the lowest GDP growth rate in the EU, at -3.3 per cent.

]]><![CDATA[European stocks extend slide as French unrest rattles investors]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/european-stocks-extend-slide-as-french-unrest-rattles-investors/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/european-stocks-extend-slide-as-french-unrest-rattles-investors/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 17:37:52 +0000European shares ended just ‌a touch lower on Tuesday, as violent protests in France kept risk appetite in check and hammered equities in the euro zone’s second-biggest economy.

The protests, ​which have intensified pressure on a country already grappling with soft economic growth and ballooning government debt, sent France’s benchmark CAC 40 index 0.38 per cent lower.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index dipped 0.14 per cent to 638.64 points after slipping 0.8 per cent in the previous session.

Investors weary of elevated oil prices ​and high government bond yields have relied on robust earnings to pluck the Stoxx 600 out of the narrow range it has been stuck ⁠in over the past month.

Dublin

Ryanair closed the session 2.6 per cent up at €23.35 as oil prices eased on news of a potential deal in the Middle East. Chief executive Michael O’Leary had earlier predicted a record increase in European air fares next year linked to higher fuel prices. The Iseq ended the day up 0.6 per cent at 14,161.

Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, O’Leary said on Tuesday during a press conference in Brussels.

Kenmare Resources, which is the subject of a potential bid by a company controlled by the Abu Dhabi royal family, saw its shares fall by 5.7 per cent to €2.66. Insulation specialist Kingspan fell 1.1 per cent to €93.95 while Kerry Group traded flat at €94.50 in advance of results later this week.

Europe

French cloud operator OVHcloud jumped 18 per cent to a near one-month high after reporting its first positive levered free cash flow since its 2021 listing.

Comet Holding jumped 4.7 per cent following an increase in the electronic equipment maker’s third-quarter sales due to expansion of data centres and AI ‌infrastructure.

Schneider Electric fell 3.3 per cent after ⁠the French electrical equipment maker raised €6 billion in an accelerated bookbuild, a fast share sale to institutional investors.

London

Britain’s FTSE 100 ended lower ‌on Tuesday as banks and commodity-linked stocks weighed, while signs of resilience in the labour market kept expectations ‌alive for a Bank of England rate hike next month.

The blue-chip FTSE 100 index fell 0.29 per cent to ​10,733.00 points, while the midcap FTSE 250 was down 0.06 per cent at 24,364.

Banks eased 0.8 per cent and hit a more than four-month low. Heavyweight lenders HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest fell between 0.8 per cent ⁠and 1.2 per cent.

Energy stocks ​also weighed on the market, with heavyweights BP ​and Shell down 1.7 per cent and 0.7 per cent, respectively

The FTSE 350 basic resources index was ‌down 1.6 per cent, with miner Anglo American ​falling 2 per cent after maintaining its 2026 copper production guidance despite a 5 per cent drop in ⁠third-quarter copper output.

Technology and online grocery firm Ocado rose 6.6 per cent to top the FTSE 250 after JP Morgan raised its price target on the stock to 460 pence from 290 pence.

New York

Wall Street’s main indexes moved higher on Tuesday as ‌a surge in healthcare stocks and softer oil prices boosted risk appetite, building on a recovery from last week’s technology-led sell-off.

Brent crude prices slipped 1.1 per cent after touching a ​five-month high in a choppy session as traders weighed Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.
