City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Wed, 21 Oct 2026 00:37:32 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 MPs voice fury after Labour rejects over a dozen proposals to boost UK investment https://www.cityam.com/mps-voice-fury-after-labour-rejects-over-a-dozen-proposals-to-boost-uk-investment/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 00:37:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2467381

MPs have voiced their frustration after the government flat out rejected more than a dozen proposals to boost lacklustre investment levels in the UK. Members of the House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee issued a list of recommendations to make the UK a more attractive destination for investment, including rejuvenating the London [...]]]>

MPs have voiced their frustration after the government flat out rejected more than a dozen proposals to boost lacklustre investment levels in the UK.

Members of the House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee issued a list of recommendations to make the UK a more attractive destination for investment, including rejuvenating the London Stock Exchange, expanding venture capital, strengthen angel investor networks and bolstering regional banking.

In response the government accepted 16 recommendations, partially accepted 18 and rejected 13. The committee said the government’s response “falls short of the coordinated reform needed” to get investment levels on a par with international competitors.

Among the proposals rejected are a review to identify a second wave of stock market reforms to boost the London Stock Exchange, changes to share stamp duty and dividend tax relief, steps to grow venture capital assets, and a consolidation of public finance institutions to boost their firepower.

Labour ‘yet to grip the scale of reform needed’

“We simply do not have institutions with enough firepower to match capital to ideas on the scale British firms need, so time after time we’re losing high potential new firms – and high paying new jobs – to American investors,” the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne, said.

“I fear ministers have yet to grip the scale of reform needed. Too often, proposals for the next stage of reform are met with a defence of what is already being done.”

“We cannot build a stronger economy without getting much more of our own capital flowing into the businesses and infrastructure that will kickstart growth.”

The inquiry received 60 written submissions and heard from 37 witnesses. Among them was the Venture Capital Trust Association (VCTA), which warned that the government’s decision to slash income tax relief for venture capital trusts to 20 per cent risked “weakening the flow of capital into the very businesses it wants to support.”

“Restoring upfront VCT income tax relief to 30 per cent would send a clear signal that the government intends to back those who take risks, build companies and create jobs,” Chris Lewis, Chair of the VCTA, said.

]]> 2467381Simon Hunt Simon Hunt Cautious trustees ‘tie the hands’ of pension schemes and hold back growth investment, industry boss says https://www.cityam.com/cautious-trustees-tie-the-hands-of-pension-schemes-and-hold-back-growth-investment-industry-boss-says/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 23:01:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2467301

Workplace pension trustees fixating on low-cost fees “tie the hands of schemes” and make it difficult for them to invest in high-growth companies, the pension trade body has said, after the government’s push to get pension money flowing into equities showed minimal progress. Zoe Alexander, chief policy officer at trade body Pensions UK, said the [...]]]>

Workplace pension trustees fixating on low-cost fees “tie the hands of schemes” and make it difficult for them to invest in high-growth companies, the pension trade body has said, after the government’s push to get pension money flowing into equities showed minimal progress.

Zoe Alexander, chief policy officer at trade body Pensions UK, said the focus on securing ultra-low fees for clients is restricting higher allocation into assets such as private equity and debt.

Her warnings came as the pensions industry updated the City on its progress toward the so-called Mansion House Compact and Accord, in which the country’s top pension money managers, including Aviva and Aegon UK, said they would allocate a chunk of their assets to private market investments.

At the time of the Accord’s launch in May last year, then Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the agreement would deliver funding for “major infrastructure, clean energy, and exciting startups”.

In the update today from the Association of British Insurers (ABI), which is administering the scheme, the 17 signatories of the Mansion House Accord were said to have allocated 3.3 per cent of assets into UK private markets by December 2025, equating to £11.1bn.

Property dominates

But so far the vast majority of committed capital has been invested into property, which dominated the allocations and came to around 70 per cent.

Signatories had invested £8bn into property and real estate, while an additional £1.3bn was invested into infrastructure. In contrast, just £500m was invested into private equity.

“If you’ve got employers and employee benefit consultants (EBCs) selecting a price [for the cost of managing schemes’ money], that then really ties the hands of schemes and makes it much harder for them to invest in these kinds of asset classes,” Alexander said in an interview with City AM, referring to investment in equities and high-growth companies.

“Which is why we really need to get the employers and EBCs…making more rounded decisions.”

Money managers who invest in venture capital and private equity typically charge higher fees than those investing in asset classes like real estate.

Yvonne Braun, director of long-term savings and health and protection policy at the ABI, said the gap between private equity and property reflected the asset’s status as a “less established” route, but argued investing in property is beneficial for the economy.

Investment-grade projects

Signatories are subject to the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) Consumer Duty and other fiduciary duties, meaning any investments must align with obligation to the saver’s financial interests.

But there is a “disparity” to how performance fees are treated depending on if a company is regulated by the FCA or The Pensions Regulator (TPR), a conflict Braun branded as “self-evidently not helpful”.

Elsewhere, Alexander raised concerns over blocked-up capital, citing the “perennial issue” of the UK lacking investment-grade growth projects.

“Trying to get the pipeline moving fast enough to come up with investment grade opportunities to make sure capital can be deployed as soon as possible…that’s a challenge,” she said.

Compact uproar

Progress against the Mansion House Compact was also lagging well behind its target, according to the update from the ABI.

The Compact was enacted in 2023, signed by 11 signatories who agreed to invest a minimum of five per cent of their default funds into unlisted equities. 

But in the three years since coming into force, total allocation has reached just 0.85 per cent, amounting to £2.7bn.

UK Private Capital executive, Michael Moore, said it was “disappointing” to see limited investment in private equity.

He said: “At the current rate of progress, the Compact target will be missed by a decade or more.

“We are in danger of missing a once-in-a-generation opportunity for sovereign UK leadership in tech and thousands of new jobs in the economy,” he said.

]]> 2467301Maisie Grice Maisie Grice Amazon pledges 30,000 jobs for Neets ahead of Budget https://www.cityam.com/amazon-pledges-30000-jobs-for-neets-ahead-of-budget/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 23:01:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2467393

Amazon has pledged to create 30,000 entry-level roles for young people by the end of the decade, in the latest sign of firms rowing in behind the government’s effort to tackle the youth unemployment crisis. The tech and retail giant has announced its “Youth Promise” programme amid growing concerns about youth joblessness and the number [...]]]>

Amazon has pledged to create 30,000 entry-level roles for young people by the end of the decade, in the latest sign of firms rowing in behind the government’s effort to tackle the youth unemployment crisis.

The tech and retail giant has announced its “Youth Promise” programme amid growing concerns about youth joblessness and the number of young people out of education, employment or training (Neet), which is now hovering just under 1m. 

Amazon’s jobs pledge will include full-time and seasonal roles, with each job to pay at least £31,000 per year.

John Boumphrey, Amazon UK’s country manager, said: “When I visit our sites, I meet young people who had no idea where to start six months ago.

“For many, Amazon was their first step into work. The Youth Promise is about reaching and supporting more people like them, in the places where those first chances are hardest to find.”

Employers have been rushing to make youth hiring pledges in recent months and pressing government to cut the costs of hiring new workers, which have rocketed since then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves ramped up national insurance contributions at the Budget in 2024.

Retailers including Tesco and Boots led a sector-wide pledge to create 100,000 new jobs, while hospitality firms including McDonald’s and Nando’s last week partnered with the government to offer 100,000 new positions for young people.

Amazon had been bracing for a potential warehouse tax at this month’s Budget, which would have pushed up business rates for online retailers to pay for tax cuts for high street shops.

But the measure was ruled out last week by Chancellor John Healey following widespread pushback from retail bosses, including John Lewis.

Healey is instead set to make online retailers like Amazon responsible for collecting tax from the sellers which use their platforms, a move which was welcomed by the US-based firm.

Work and pensions secretary Pat McFadden said: “[Amazon’s] Youth Promise will help thousands of young people take their first step into work, with good pay, real support and a clear route to progress. 

“This is exactly the kind of employer leadership that will reach young people in the communities that need it the most and drive our economy forward.”

Tech firms in work experience pledge

On Wednesday, the government said it would separately offer 10,000 work experience placements in the UK’s digital and tech sector. 

The scheme is being backed by some of the country’s biggest tech employers, including Microsoft, Cisco, IBM and Cognizant. 

The government said tech companies should back up this programme by offering more full-time roles, urging the sector to provide 20,000 entry-level jobs each year.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: “It’s one of the biggest frustrations when you’re starting out. Everyone tells you that you need experience to get a job, but nobody gives you the chance to get that experience in the first place.

“Thousands of young people will get the chance to get their foot in the door in one of the UK’s biggest growth sectors, build their confidence and skills, and get something meaningful on their CV.”

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, said: “Our country is grappling [with] a generational challenge – we cannot and will not let our young people be locked out of the British workforce.

“Getting a good job in our thriving digital and tech industry shouldn’t be determined by where you live or what school you go to.”

]]> 2467393Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong High School Musical London review: autumn’s must-book sing-a-long https://www.cityam.com/high-school-musical-review-autumns-must-book-sing-a-long/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 23:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2467468

High School Musical review and star rating: ★★★★ Musicals have always looked to film and TV for inspiration, and nostalgia is increasingly a driver for commissioners. West End productions of Clueless, The Devil Wears Prada and 50 First Dates have belted their way over from Hollywood, although the announcement of a musical version of High [...]]]>

High School Musical review and star rating: ★★★★

Musicals have always looked to film and TV for inspiration, and nostalgia is increasingly a driver for commissioners. West End productions of Clueless, The Devil Wears Prada and 50 First Dates have belted their way over from Hollywood, although the announcement of a musical version of High School Musical felt more surprising. 

While there are undoubtedly HSM diehards, with this stage adaptation, even fans of the original film are asking, “why now?” The Zac Efron movies are generous, frothy fun, but perhaps don’t ironically translate to adult viewing in quite the same way as other noughties classics.

Whatever the case, despite this stage adaptation chiming with the 20th anniversary of the first film, this musical feels like a left-field booking for the Troubadour Theatre, the new 2,000 capacity venue in Wembley whose last show, Starlight Express, was an Andrew Lloyd Webber smash hit. 

High School Musical: Zingy choreography

Anyway, it turns out everybody wants to see High School Musical, the musical, with a script from David Simpatico and musical arrangements from producer Bryan Louiselle: tickets for this new production are nearly sold out for my preview performance.

First off, the new Troubadour Theatre is an astonishing gain for London theatre. It is re-purposing the former TV studios that hosted the live recordings of The X Factor, and the same shiny floor glamour from the building’s TV days is retained in this expensive-looking adaptation.

As for the show, this isn’t an immersive gimmick like you might think, but a real piece of theatre, even if we’re initially thrown into a set up involving audience engagement. Cheerleaders are engaging with the audience from the stage before the ‘show’ begins, and in this impressive space, you feel like you’re about to watch a live recording of Simon Cowell’s defunct reality show, or at least something major and televisual: everything’s enormous, from the sky-high lighting rigs to the East High wall hangings and full-size basketball court which forms the stage.

Glistening production

It’s a precursor to co-directors Joseph Houston and William Whelton’s glistening, exciting production that does justice to the original film’s energy and youthful vigour.

This adaptation is mostly a blow-by-blow account of the original film, although there are a few new scenes, which I won’t spoil here, other than to say nothing fundamentally changes the plot. One thought about David Simpatico’s script: there is a missed opportunity for the character of Ryan to come out as gay. Original High School Musical director Kenny Ortega stated in 2020 that he was intended to be LGBTQ in the film, but it was felt that Disney weren’t ready to back a gay lead in 2006. So it’s a shame Ryan doesn’t quite get to rewrite history here. 

Anyway, as a production as a whole, this is a zingy, well choreographed, well sung adaptation of the story that follows high school stud Troy Bolton as he attempts to balance his commitments to the school’s basketball team with his new interest in performing in the high school musical. All the while, he’s navigating his crush on school friend Gabriella.

Glued to Caitlin Tipping

While Tobias Turley and Leonor Correia belt well as the central couple, it can be hard to get a read on their Troy and Gabriella. Their shyness is partly the point – neither leads are the most charismatic characters in the film – but still, these lovers should sparkle more with playful energy and personality.

I was glued to Caitlin Tipping’s Sharpay Evans, the majorly extroverted singer always trying to get Troy’s attention. Tipping’s Sharpay is posher and more statuesque, and slightly more eccentric in her mannerisms, but a solid comic performance is backed up by equally stonking vocals. She’s brilliant in a similar way as she was during her turn as Celine Dion recently in Titanique. Luke Bayer’s Ryan Evans is fairly true to the film: you endure to his vulnerable, likeable Ryan. 

The two major pulls are the musical numbers and the adult cast, though, which features former McFly singer Harry Judd and former film cast member Kaycee Stroh, who played Martha Cox in the movies and has graduated into the arts teacher Ms Darbus for the stage adaptation. Stroh is so much fun as the pretentious, always gesticulating creative, who argues airily about how the arts are more important than sports when it comes to vying for Troy’s time. Stroh brings texture and depth, though, and never plays it as caricature. Judd is better than you might think in conveying emotion as Troy’s slightly toxic dad-cum-basketball coach.

Vivid, playful choreography

As for those song-and-dance scenes, well, the tracks still sound killer, Aaron Renfree’s vivid, playful choreography translating them sparklingly onto the stage, though I found the crowd surprisingly sedate. The production never encourages standing, even for the closing numbers, even though the main tracks, including Stick to the Status Quo, Breaking Free and We’re All In This Together have dated brilliantly. 

Still, everyone finally gets a chance to stand up and sing and dance when the production essentially crow bars in a final reprieve of all the major numbers so that everyone can film them. That’s the only disappointing bit; I rather enjoyed when phones were in our pockets and we were all in this together, like the song told us to be. It’s a shame to dilute the end of the story for the sake of an Instagram moment, but hey, that’s the world we live in. Still, a minor gripe about an altogether gleaming adaptation.

High School Musical plays at the Troubadour Theatre until 3 January 2027

Natwest is facing backlash from trade union Unite over a new plan to require workers to attend the office for a mandatory two days a week. On Tuesday Unite, which represents over 1 million workers across private, public, and voluntary sectors, including some Natwest employees, said the lender’s decision was “out of touch with the [...]]]>

Natwest is facing backlash from trade union Unite over a new plan to require workers to attend the office for a mandatory two days a week.

On Tuesday Unite, which represents over 1 million workers across private, public, and voluntary sectors, including some Natwest employees, said the lender’s decision was “out of touch with the realities facing its workforce.”

From February next year, all employees at the bank will be required to work from the office for two days a week.

Some employees at the FTSE 100 bank who are ‘remote-first’ workers are currently required to attend the office for two days a month, which will no longer be the case when the new policy comes into force.

It is the latest example of firms calling workers back into the office after widespread work from home orders during the pandemic.

But Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the move is “yet another kick in the teeth for workers who have suffered years of real-terms pay cuts and who are struggling to make ends meet.”

“Natwest’s decision is completely out of touch with the realities facing its workforce. Thousands of workers face higher travel and childcare costs and disruption to caring responsibilities,” Graham said.

Natwest ‘must ditch’ office attendance plans

Graham added Natwest “must ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers.”

 “For Natwest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce,” Graham said.

Nearly 17,300 staff at the bank follow a hybrid working pattern where they are required to attend the office at least three days a fortnight, and a further 13,500 are remote-first, roles which are only required to attend the office twice a month.

The remainder of its UK staff, which includes those in customer facing roles, those working in branches, and other customer-facing roles including traders, must already go in to the office least four days a week.

“We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we’re giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition,” a Natwest spokesman said.

“Flexible working remains an important part of how we work, but we’ve also learnt more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers,” the spokesperson added.

]]> 2467423Rosie Harris-Davison Rosie Harris-Davison Nscale eyes second $45bn deal with Anthropic after Microsoft setback https://www.cityam.com/nscale-eyes-second-45bn-deal-with-anthropic-after-microsoft-setback/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 15:55:37 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2467324

British AI infrastructure firm, Nscale, is in talks to secure a second $45bn (£33.5bn) computing deal with Anthropic, just a day after Microsoft pulled out of its flagship UK data centre project. The Nvidia-backed company is negotiating an agreement to supply the US AI giant with computing power from a second facility at its Monarch [...]]]>

British AI infrastructure firm, Nscale, is in talks to secure a second $45bn (£33.5bn) computing deal with Anthropic, just a day after Microsoft pulled out of its flagship UK data centre project.

The Nvidia-backed company is negotiating an agreement to supply the US AI giant with computing power from a second facility at its Monarch campus in West Virginia. The proposed deal would cover 460 megawatts of capacity powered by Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips, potentially doubling Anthropic’s Nscale commitments to almost $90bn.

The agreement could be signed within days, though discussions remain ongoing and terms could change, as reported by Bloomberg.

The talks follow an initial $44.6bn agreement signed in August, under which Anthropic agreed to lease computing capacity from the same West Virginia campus over six years.

The potential contract comes at a critical moment for London-founded Nscale, which is preparing for a blockbuster New York stock market listing amid growing scrutiny of the vast sums being spent on AI infrastructure.

The company reportedly targets a valuation of up to $30bn, although some investors have pushed for a lower figure between $16bn and $19bn.

Nscale and Anthropic have not commented on this deal.

Nscale faces mounting pressure ahead of IPO

The negotiations come just a day after Microsoft withdrew from plans to develop what was billed as Britain’s largest AI data centre in Loughton, Essex, dealing a blow to one of the UK’s flagship AI infrastructure projects.

The £2bn development, announced last year and championed by the government, has been delayed by issues with its electricity grid connection.

Nscale said it remained committed to the project despite Microsoft’s withdrawal.

“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts”, a spokesperson said.

Microsoft also stressed that the decision related to a single site, adding that it remained committed to its wider partnership with Nscale.

The setback has raised questions about the company’s ability to deliver its ambitious data centre pipeline. Last week, Bloomberg reported that construction at Nscale’s flagship Norwegian facility in Glomfjord was six months behind schedule following technical problems, including cooling system leaks and a fire.

The company reported a $1bn net loss on $141m in revenue in the first half of 2026, while its IPO filings showed it had yet to secure financing for the infrastructure needed to fulfil its first Anthropic contract.

Under that agreement, Anthropic can terminate the deal if Nscale fails to meet certain financing and operational milestones.

The proposed second contract would therefore represent a significant vote of confidence in Nscale’s expansion plans, although the company would still need to secure funding for the additional computing infrastructure.

The talks also underscore the growing financial commitments underpinning the AI boom, as developers race to secure the computing power needed to train and run more advanced models.

Anthropic has struck several multibillion-dollar infrastructure agreements as demand for its Claude AI models grows, while investors have become increasingly concerned about the debt and execution risks facing data centre developers.

US tech firm Clearview AI is challenging a UK privacy watchdog ruling that found it breached GDPR rules by collecting and using images of UK residents scraped from the internet and social media.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) imposed a £7.5m fine on the US-based tech company in May 2022 and asked it to delete UK residents’ data after finding it had used images of people in the UK that were collected from social media and the web to create a global online database to be used for facial recognition.

The ICO also ordered the AI company, which builds and sells a database of images used for facial recognition technology primarily for law enforcement and government agencies outside the UK, to stop scraping and using UK residents’ personal data.

Clearview appealed the fine and enforcement notice, bringing legal proceedings to the First-Tier Tribunal in 2023 and arguing the data watchdog lacked power to enforce against a company operating in a different jurisdiction; the court ruled in its favour.

However, in October 2025, the Upper Tribunal overturned the decision after the ICO appealed. The court ruled that the regulator had jurisdiction over the US tech firm and could enforce against it, establishing that Clearview AI obtaining and storing images of UK residents constituted ‘behavioural monitoring’ under the GDPR.

The tech firm was at the Court of Appeal on Tuesday and Wednesday as it sought to overturn the Upper Tribunal ruling and reinstate the First-Tier Tribunal ruling.

Decision may have ‘implications’ for AI firms

Nicola Cain, chief executive and principal consultant at legal consultancy firm Handley Gill, told City AM the decision may have implications for AI companies which carry out similar activities.

“While Clearview AI’s appeal against the £7.5m penalty imposed by the ICO is on a technical point of law relating to whether, as a foreign entity, it is subject to the UK GDPR and required to protect the personal data of individuals in the UK, the principles involved have a wide application, with implications for AI developers, data brokers and database operators who scrape and aggregate personal information from the internet and share it for purposes including AI training.

“Should the ICO prevail in its argument that systematic scraping of online data constitutes behavioural monitoring, the Clearview AI fine may just be the first of many,” Cain added.

An ICO spokesperson said as the hearing “forms part of ongoing legal proceedings in relation to the £7.5m monetary penalty and enforcement notice we issued to Clearview AI Inc. in 2022” it “would not be appropriate for the Information Commission to comment further while the case is before the court.”

Clearview AI was contacted for comment.

Barclays‘ investment bank could be in line for another major boost. But Samuel Norman takes a look at the progress investors will be wanting to hear on its latest strategy plans.

When CS Venkatakrishnan laid out his sweeping restructuring of Barclays he promised a “simpler, better and more balanced” bank. 

Key to this was reducing reliance on investment banking operations, which had proven to be a volatile source of revenue due to its unpredictability across dealmaking and trading. 

Speaking at the beginning of 2024, Venkat said the investment bank has to be “higher returning” but also become a “smaller part of Barclays”. 

Unfortunately for Venkatakrishnan, known in the industry as Venkat, market tensions have kept the investment bank centre stage across the group – and come Thursday it will be under the spotlight during the group’s third-quarter update.

Last year, the investment bank made up 44 per cent of the group’s revenue, thanks largely to the market chaos triggered by President Donald Trump’s tariff trade offensive. Even while traditional deal advisory lagged, trading desks made hay, with equities income rising 12 per cent to £3.2bn. 

In the first half of 2026, there were new geopolitical tensions, same outcome. Barclays investment banking division saw its income climb 11 per cent year-on-year to £8bn for the first half of the year. 

Equities income soared 45 per cent to £1.3bn in the second quarter alone as traders capitalised on the market swings and volatility drawn out by the Middle East conflict. Investment bank income grew as a share for the group to 48.4 per cent. 

The geopolitical crises may have derailed Venkat’s hopes to make investment banking operations a smaller share of the bank, but his strategy to tighten the balance sheet has worked behind the scenes.

The bank chief made no specific target around revenue share but instead pledged to bring return on tangible equity (RoTE) for the investment bank in line with the wider group. RoTE is a key profitability ratio, measuring a company’s net income relative to the average value of a company’s common equity.

By the end of the year, Venkat has hoped to bring it in line with a broader group target of 12 per cent from around seven per cent in 2023.

In 2025, RoTE reached 10.6 per cent and for the first half of 2026 surpassed 15.5 per cent. This follows the bank bearing the axe on costs in the division with its cost-to-income ratio improving significantly to 54 per cent in the first half, compared to 62 per cent in 2025.

No investors will be assessing Venkat’s larger ambition where he looks to extend RoTE above 14 per cent by 2028.

Another big target for scrutiny on Thursday will be progress on risk-weighted assets (RWA), a key measure of the overall size and financial risk of its loans and investments. Analysts expect Barclays investment bank will hold around 55 per cent of the group’s  RWA following the third quarter.

Venkat pledged to bring this down to “around” 50 per cent by the end of 2026 in a bid to boost the firm’s stock price and free up capital for returns. Analysts expect the investment bank’s share will remain around 55.14 per cent for the year-end.

In an update earlier this year, Venkat was bolder in his promises. The bank chief said the share would be reduced to 50 per cent by 2028 – something internal analysts believe is achievable, pencilling in 50.73 per cent

Barclays fights to pump up stock price

The original strategy has been centred on boosting Barclays’ share price, which has lagged its counterparts in recent years. Just weeks before the bank unveiled its overhaul years ago, Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund cut its stake in the firm, amplifying fears around returns.

But investors have rewarded the manoeuvres with Barclays share price up 150 per cent since the February 2024 overhaul – notwithstanding some steep losses on account of the geopolitical turmoil.

To drum up further excitement, Barclays laid out plans in February to return more than £15bn to shareholders through dividends and buybacks by 2028. 

The quarter due to report on Thursday is forecast to be another win for Barclays with analysts expecting pre-tax profit to rise to £2.4bn from £2bn the year prior.

But the investment bank threatens to steal the spotlight once more – if Wall Street’s reporting season is anything to go by.

The US’ big six – that’s JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo – reaped a $22bn trading revenue haul in the third quarter.

“Barclays and UBS are set to be the outperformers among Europeans,” says Philip Richards, senior industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence.

Richards added as a whole Barclays revenue momentum was expected to “remain robust” in the third-quarter keeping Venkat’s 14 per cent RoTE target “within reach”.

Global instability may have stopped Venkat from reining in the investment bank’s dominance but the bank chief will need to show his grip on long-term targets isn’t loosening to keep investors on side.

The New-York listed firm will restructure its UK and Ireland division, slashing around 15 per cent of its workforce. 

Redundancies will affect roles in Leeds and Dublin, as well as Portugal and Romania where staff support the UK division.

The betting group said the losses were in response to the “significant increase” in UK gambling taxes announced in last year’s Autumn Budget.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves nearly doubled the charge, hiking them from 21 per cent to 40 per cent. The changes took effect this April, and bookmakers are now bracing for a levy on their profits to rise from 15 per cent to 25 per cent from April 2027.

Kevin Harrington, Flutter’s UK&I chief executive, said the gambling industry “cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base”.

Recent tax hikes on the sector have “fundamentally changed the economic model of the regulated betting and gaming industry in the UK while helping to fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market,” he added.

The Office for Budget Responsibility warned in November 2025 that gamblers moving towards illegal gambling websites in the wake of hikes could also reduce the expected tax take by around £500m.

On the chopping block

Flutter owns high-street bookmaker Paddy Power as well as Sky Bet, Betfair and Tombola. It employs 8,960 people in the UK and Ireland division.

Its redundancy plans follow previous warnings from the gambling giant that it would take a £400m hit from Labour’s tax hikes in April 2027, ultimately forcing it to look for ways to cut costs.

The latest wave of layoffs also come on top of plans announced last month to review 100 Paddy Power betting shops, putting around 400 jobs at risk. But Flutter said those shops were not affected by its latest redundancy announcement.

Flutter’s share price has tumbled 64.5 per cent since the start of the year, trading at $77.3 (£57.8).

Bookies feel the heat

Other bookmakers have also blamed Labour’s tax raid for forcing them to trim headcounts and close physical stores.

William Hill closed 270 shops in April while Betfred announced 132 closures in July, impacting 600 workers.

Bet365 also unveiled around 340 redundancies in September, while Ladbrokers-owner Entain proposed cutting 400 customer service jobs. 

Healey is reportedly deciding whether to raise machine gaming duty, the taxes levied on slot machines on the Autumn Budget.

Six gambling bosses, including Harrington, wrote to the Chancellor last week urging him against further hikes and to halt next year’s planned increase to betting duty. 

They warned doing so could lead to as many as 15,9000 job losses, as well 1,470 shop closures and 34 casino closures.

As the Toast the City Awards approaches, we’re looking at some of the cultural highlights in the Square Mile that could take home a coveted Slice of Toast. Today we look at Finalist Dr Johnson’s House and the new Blue Plaque for his brilliant mentee Francis Barber.

Doctor Johnson’s House is a worthy Finalist in our Toast the City Awards. But did you know there is another fascinating cultural figure linked to the site – and that you can visit it right now?

Dr Samuel Johnson will be a name recognisable to many – he was a writer, critic and lexicographer perhaps best known for writing A Dictionary of the English Language in 1755, an incredibly important work that helped define the way the English language was thought of and studied. He resided at what we now call Dr Johnson’s House in Gough Square in Fleet Street Quarter, a Grade I-listed late 17th-century building that he rented for 11 years (it became a museum in 1912).

Dro Johnson’s House was the first landmark in the City of London to be given a Blue Plaque, earning the accolade 150 years ago. Now another Blue Plaque joins it – one dedicated to Francis Barber, Dr Johnson’s servant, friend and heir who would become Britain’s first black school teacher.

The wonderful Francis Barber

Barber, a West African man born into slavery in Jamaica, came to London as a child and lived at Dr Johnson’s house from 1752 to 1756, working there as his servant. Dr Johnson supported him and his family and helped secure his financial future, including making Barber the sole heir and beneficiary of a trust established in his will, something that was sadly controversial at the time.

Dr Johnson’s House is now a charity that runs a museum at the site and is believed to be the only surviving property in the City that was home to a formerly enslaved person who later lived there as a free man.

Of the 140 plaques in the Square Mile, most of them commemorate institutions and organisations, such as the Samaritans, the Great Synagogue and Royal College of Physicians, with only 32 plaques representing individuals. Following a comprehensive review, the scheme has been redesigned to provide a modern, transparent, and inclusive process with clear guidance, embedded equality, equity, diversity and inclusion principles.

While each plaque will be funded primarily by applicants or their sponsors, a new annual City of London Corporation funding pot will support at least one outstanding application each year.

Brendan Barns, chair of the City of London Corporation’s Culture, Heritage and Libraries Committee, said: “Our Blue Plaques Scheme makes a welcome return and highlights the City of London Corporation’s renewed commitment to commemorating remarkable people, places and institutions that have shaped the Square Mile.

“It is our hope that the redesigned scheme will attract thoughtful and persuasively-written applications from a wide range of backgrounds, all of them reminding us that, behind every Blue Plaque is a story worth telling.”

Celine Luppo McDaid, the Hyde director of Dr Johnson’s House, said: “We are thrilled to celebrate the remarkable life of Francis Barber with this Blue Plaque. Enslaved on a Jamaican plantation, Barber came to London and, in this house, he learned to read and write, going on to become the first Black teacher in British history. His story is central to our commitment to bringing long-overlooked lives into the present day.

“As the House of Words, Dr Johnson’s House explores and represents the experiences and legacies of Francis Barber and the extraordinary people who were living here in the middle of the 18th century. By engaging with issues such as friendship, grief, gender, identity, slavery and mental health, the lives of those who went before us resonate with our 21st century audiences.”

Andy Burnham and John Healey have spoken at length about efforts to provide “breathing space” to both households and businesses. This task at next week’s Budget has now become more difficult. 

Over the summer the jobs market continued to weaken. Workers are at risk of being worse off while job seekers are finding it harder to secure new gigs and hiring appetite cools. 

Including bonuses, wage growth continued to slow, falling to 3.7 per cent. When bonuses are excluded, the annualised growth in average weekly earnings remained at the lowest level in six years. 

These earnings are partly satisfactory to the Bank of England, which worries about a spike in wages fuelling higher prices set by firms. Although they remain far lower than public sector pay settlements, private sector earnings growth is at a level consistent with the Bank of England’s target to reach two per cent inflation in the medium term. 

However, what might worry the government more than it does the Monetary Policy Committee is the narrowing growth of wages in real terms. Annual pay growth adjusted for inflation was 0.6 per cent, far lower than the levels of over two per cent seen when Labour was elected into power in mid-2024. 

This pay squeeze is at the nub of the cost of living pressures that Healey is concerned about. 

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at the consulting firm RSM UK said it was “extremely likely” that private sector workers were set to take a “real terms pay cut” in the coming months as inflation rises higher above three per cent. 

“That will intensify the pressure on Burnham and Healey to come up with a package to support the cost of living in the Budget next week,” Pugh said. 

The challenge Healey has, which is not particular to this chancellor, is that he has little room for manoeuvre. His fiscal headroom is projected to have been halved to around £12bn. Healey has ruled out some revenue-raisers in the forms of a capital gains tax hike. A banking tax is expected to be the main new generator of income for the Chancellor. 

Pugh said the “most likely course is a series of temporary measures designed to blunt the worst of the coming rise in utility bills and inflation, without affecting the fiscal headroom in 2029-30”. 

Healey’s unemployment boost

Healey has something to celebrate. The unemployment rate dropped to 4.7 per cent in the the three-month period between June and August. That fell from a rate of 4.9 per cent previously. Some economists in the City had warned that the unemployment rate was on an upward trajectory, rising to as high as 5.7 per cent in the coming months. 

While joblessness levels could yet rise as a result of cost pressures biting business owners, the lower rate in unemployment, coupled with a slight rise in wage growth, could provide some reprieve to the Chancellor. 

“The Chancellor may also have more room for manoeuvre in next week’s Budget than previously feared,” WPI Strategy economist Martin Beck said. 

“Stronger-than-expected growth and inflation-boosted tax receipts could limit the need for significant tax rises, potentially creating scope for targeted measures such as cutting employers’ National Insurance contributions for younger workers.”

Beck added that the UK economy was not in the midst of an “employment crisis” and rather the jobs market was “stuck in the slow lane”. It may be in the government’s powers to get it firing again.

Apple introduced a system allowing third-party developers to access its contactless technology in Britain in 2024, but the CMA said no rival wallet-type product had launched through the arrangement.

However, alternative payment services from providers including Paypal and Klarna have launched in the EU following regulatory intervention.

“Digital wallets are becoming an increasingly important way for people to pay, so we welcome the CMA’s focus on promoting effective competition in this area,” a spokesperson for banking trade body UK Finance said.

They added the open access to NFC functionality on Apple’s operating systems would support innovation “reduce reliance on a single wallet provider.”

The watchdog is proposing that Apple support both major international NFC standards, rather than the single approach currently available to UK developers.

Setting foot inside Restaurant St Barts is one of the most discombobulating experiences I’ve had arriving for dinner. There are quicker ways to get there. I missed a turn and had to loop around, but the added chaos of high-summer Thirsty Thursday in the City made the arrival in this intensely serene restaurant all the more remarkable. 

The space really is something. From the entrance it opens up in a Scandi-style sweep of wood, linens and light. Chairs in the bar area are burnished with sheepskins and the walls are brutal with concrete lit by mounted candles. But as the restaurant unfurls, past the open kitchen with its driftwood ephemera of drying meats, fruits and stacks of fermenting jars, and into the main dining room, the whole space opens onto the medieval church of St Bartholomew the Great, which dates back to 1123. Nowhere mixes past and present quite like the City.

For executive chef and co-founder Johnnie Crowe, the location is a big part of the restaurant’s draw.

“It really feels like an escape from the city,” he tells me. 

“I think experience-led restaurants like ours need to have an element of intrigue and excitement about every aspect of the experience, and the location we have definitely does that.”

St Barts is a Michelin-starred restaurant that only uses British ingredients in its tasting menus. Crowe, who co-founded St Barts in 2022 with Luke Wasserman and Toby Neill, has built a restaurant around his producers. Before Barts, the trio owned Nest in Shoreditch, which this summer was transformed into the much-lauded and much-Instagrammed British bistro Tavern. But St Barts is where Crowe’s dogged devotion to homegrown suppliers pushes him to put out a seriously unique menu. 

“Our suppliers are the main focus of the restaurant. We’ve spent years building up our relationships and researching new and different people who grow, fish and farm. It allows us to do what we do and be 100 per cent British to the core,” he says.

As with all good meals, dinner at St Barts starts with snacks and cocktails. A martini briny with sea fennel rather than olives is paired with beautifully fatty drapes of house-cured coppa (‘gabagool’ in The Sopranos). Next comes a bomb cheese and onion tart, and then a quail liver parfait on a sort of Hobnob that would also make an amazing pudding. As you move into the church-framed dining room, the table is made up to look like a 17th-century still life of summer’s bounty. A nest of quail eggs, sugar snap peas, a block of pork fat, ears of corn, crab shells, a tangle of red currants. 

It’s here in the dining room that the relationship with British producers – and the way it slips and slides between the familiar and unexpected – really shines. 

The first half of the tasting menu features a dish of peas. The peas, grassy, bittersweet and yet perfectly toothsome, are as good as any in the world. It makes sense for Crowe to centre a dish on them. Glistening in a lovage oil – the most medieval of hardy herbs – the peas top a lardo chawanmushi. Peas, pork and plant: this dish feels so rooted in the British larder (that said, it paired amazingly with a Nikolaihof Grüner Veltliner from Austria that tasted like an extinguished sparkler – wine and coffee are, thankfully, exceptions to the rule). 

Later, quail with a bruising mole (a deeply aromatic Mexican sauce) is served on a plate scattered with little picky bits. It’s a fun, slightly kitschy, squirrel plate of exceptional ingredients, including a heart, a big blackberry and a nasturtium leaf. But the star – and one of the best things I’ve eaten all year – is a side of corn. Crowe makes butter from dried corn and then folds things through fresh British corn which has been barbecued on the cob. 

But then a lobster dish totally upended my expectations of British produce. Served in two parts, it starts with a rich nest of Singapore-leaning noodles, and ends with the tail served with quinoa. The real surprise in both was the sansho, a highly floral, zesty Japanese pepper, which makes the sweet richness of lobster zip. Crowe told me it’s grown in Lewes.

“We source it from Namayasai Farm. Ikuyo, who runs the farm, is incredible. We depend on her for so many different products and absolutely love working with her.”

The UK has more niche suppliers and green-fingered enthusiasts than we give credit for. So perhaps the biggest challenge for a restaurant using solely British ingredients is moving with the ebb and flow of the seasons. As we move through autumn and into winter, corn and peas fade to memory. Crowe plays with fermentation and pickling to stretch the seasons. Meat trim is turned to garum, cherry blossoms and elderflowers are suspended in jars, and “Pink Flamingo peas” from Norfolk are transformed into miso.

So it’s perhaps St Barts’ pudding and signature dish that distils Crowe’s cooking ethos so fully. Barley is inoculated with koji and left to ferment and blacken for a couple of months, producing a chocolatey product that’s then blitzed into a roasty, bitter-rich ganache. The barley is also used to make an ice cream, a caramel and a tuile. Out of a single grain Crowe squeezes out one of the tastiest desserts in London. And when paired with the Domaine de Rancy, a bread and butter vin doux naturel, it’s practically unbeatable. 

Leaving the gentle hold of St Barts and returning to the pint-smashed City is an adjustment. I hope to return soon to see what Crowe can make of the colder, shorter days, and to discover more than I thought possible when it comes to homegrown.

The Toast the City Awards are mere days away – we ask if Whitechapel Gallery has what it takes to bring home a coveted Slice of Toast.

The Whitechapel Gallery is one of the undisputed cultural heavyweights of the Square Mile. Having opened in 1901, with a stunning building designed by the architect Charles Harrison Townsend, it was among London’s first publicly funded galleries. Its mission statement was to democratise the often class-locked art world, bringing “the finest art of the world” to the people of the East End.

It was popular from the get-go, with its debut exhibition, Modern Pictures by Living Artists, Pre-Raphaelites and Old Masters, drawing some 260,000 visitors, although legend has it this was in part down to the novelty of seeing electric lighting as much as the appeal of those Old Masters.

This year marked the Whitechapel Gallery’s 125th year, making it a particularly apt time to look back at its triumphs. There is perhaps no 20th century painting more iconic than Picasso’s Guernica, which has been exhibited in the UK just once… at the Whitechapel Gallery in 1939. Other important artists to have been proudly displayed here include Jackson Pollock, with a 1958 exhibition representing his first major British show, Mark Rothko, who also had his first British show here in 1961, and Frida Kahlo, who was displayed here in 1982, years before she became a household name.

The Whitechapel Gallery in the 1970s onwards

The ascendancy continued in the 1970s and 80s, with artistic director Nicholas Serota (who would go on to be artistic director of the Tate) maintaining its reputation as a leading cultural hotspot. In 2007 the gallery embarked upon a two year redevelopment that greatly increased its display space and helped develop its offering as a community hub, creating an archive and reading room.

Its 125th year has seen exhibitions including Joy Gregory: Catching Flies with Honey, which ran from October 2025 into early 2026; Veronica Ryan: Multiple Conversations (1 April-14 June); Backyard Biennial: East (15 July-6 September); and Cecilia Vicuña: Living Threads (7 October-14 February 2027). 

While it has some fearsome competition in the form of the Barbican, Guildhall, the Bank of England Museum and more, Whitechapel Gallery is a clear contender for one of our coveted Slices of Toast at the 2026 Toast the City Awards.

Team GB Olympic gold medallist Jade Jones has announced a multi-million-pound investment in a UK wellness brand.

Her firm, JJ Double Gold, will invest in York-based CBD business HempWell Ltd over the next three years, Jones having started her own brand in July.

Welsh athlete Jones, nicknamed the Headhunter, won Team GB’s first Olympic medal in taekwondo at the London 2012 Games before retaining her title four years later in Rio de Janeiro.

Jade Jones in CBD move

As the Toast the City Awards party nears, we have spoken to some of our favourite nominees – this week we chatted to Shoe Lane Library manager Sona Kalenderian.

Introduce yourself and Shoe Lane Library

My name is Ovssanna Kalenderian but I’m known as Sona by everyone including our customers. I the manager of Shoe Lane Library, which is part of Barbican & Community Libraries. I’ve been with Shoe Lane Library for 25 of its 44 years.

What makes Shoe Lane Library stand out?

We’ve had customers describe our library as a “hidden gem” and a “family hub”. People often tell us how friendly, welcoming and caring we are, and that coming to the library makes them feel at home.

One Japanese family became particularly close to us while they were living in London for two years, while the husband was studying for his master’s degree. They told us they thought of us as family. Before returning to Japan, they came in especially to say goodbye and take a photo with us as a memory. That was really touching.

Another Japanese couple stayed in London for just three months. After they returned home, they made a YouTube video about the three places they recommended visiting in London. We couldn’t believe it when we found out that Shoe Lane Library was number two, alongside the Royal Opera House and Sky Garden! We only discovered this because another Japanese family who uses the library saw the video and translated it for me. We were absolutely delighted.

What’s the one thing Shoe Lane Library better than anyone else?

For us, the library is much more than somewhere to borrow a book. It’s a safe place, a sanctuary and somewhere people can feel comfortable and welcome. People come here to study, read, work, learn, meet others or simply have somewhere to be.

We also offer lots of community and wellbeing activities. Our Dragon Café in the City, for example, has been running since 2018. Every other Wednesday, our partners Mental Fight Club deliver Wellness Wednesday, supporting people with their mental health and wellbeing.

We also have reading groups, children’s and adult’s events and many other activities. There really is something for everyone.

What’s been your biggest challenge?

Our biggest challenge after Covid was getting our visitor numbers back up. With so many people working from home and spending less time in the office, fewer people were coming into the library.

So, we thought, how can we bring people back? We started organising lots of different events for adults and children, and I networked with people and organisations to find interesting speakers. We’ve had some fantastic guests, including an Australian screenwriter and film producer.

We are very lucky because people are so generous with their time. We never charge our customers. Everything we do is free and open to everyone.

How has the Square Mile changed?

When I first started, the Square Mile was buzzing with City workers, and we welcomed at least 800 customers a day. The library was incredibly busy. I really miss that atmosphere and would love to see that kind of buzz again.

What’s a small detail you obsess over that your visitors might not notice?

For me, it’s the small things. Is everything tidy? Do the displays look good? Has everyone been welcomed with a smile? Customers might not notice those details, but I do! I want people to walk in and immediately feel that they belong here.    

Who is your typical customer?

I wouldn’t say we have a typical customer. Our community is very multicultural and diverse, and everyone is welcome. Whether someone visits us regularly or walks in for the first time, we want them to feel at home and part of our community.

What’s one trend you’re embracing – and one you’re ignoring?

The trend we’re embracing is turning the library into a community and wellbeing space, not just somewhere for books. The trend I’m ignoring is moving everything online. Technology is useful, but for me, libraries are still about people. That face-to-face connection, a friendly welcome and making someone feel at home are things technology can’t replace.

Which other City venues do you rate highly?

I’d say the Barbican Centre and Guildhall Art Gallery. They are fantastic cultural spaces, and I really admire the way they engage with different audiences. I’m also very proud of our Barbican & Community Libraries and the work we do within our communities.             

What do you like to have on your toast?

Grilled bacon.

If you spend long enough in London, especially around Canary Wharf, you become accustomed to noticing some very nice cars driving amidst the shadows of glass towers, writes our motoring journalist, Tim Barnes-Clay

Audi RS e-tron GTs, Porsche Taycans, and the occasional Aston Martin or Bentley are commonly seen.

Now Polestar – the Swedish automotive marque that makes premium, design-led electric cars – is offering professionals something a tad different to drive around in.

The new Polestar 5 is an electric grand tourer that blends supercar performance with the luxury and long-distance competence you might expect from a high-end legacy whip.

And Polestar UK Managing Director Matt Galvin has a good idea of who will want it.

“I’d say it’s the thinking man’s Porsche Taycan,” he tells me.

That is a confident statement, but after sampling both flavours of the Polestar 5, I can see why he makes the comparison.

Style and Substance

Developed from the Precept concept with surprisingly few changes, the production car has a slick, aviation-inspired form and is made from bonded aluminium.

The four-door vehicle is light and rigid, and Polestar claims it has torsional rigidity superior to that of a two-seater sports car or supercar. 

But even without all that, I’d still want the low-slung Polestar 5 for its looks alone.

Fortunately, it delivers on all fronts.

Sharp and Capable

I drove the Polestar 5 Dual Motor and Performance versions, and the former isn’t exactly slow.

Indeed, describing it as the more levelheaded of the two doesn’t do it justice.

It is pin-you-to-your-seat quick, yet exquisitely controlled. Point the car towards a sequence of bends, and it slices through them like a laser through frosted glass, with the chassis feeling calm and planted beneath your backside.

The 550kW (737bhp) Dual Motor delivers 812Nm of torque and does the sacred 0-60mph in 3.8 seconds. That’s enough to make overtaking on a British A or B-road almost preposterously easy.

The only slight fly in the ointment for me is the front seats – they feel a little firm.

That is where the Performance version gets interesting. Its more advanced MagneRide adaptive damping gives the 5 a smoother ride, easing the seats’ firmness and making the overall driving experience feel more sumptuous.

Peachy Performance

And yet, the Polestar 5 Performance version borders on beautifully unhinged.

The numbers give you more than a hint of what it’s capable of before you even sit in it. With 650kW (871bhp), 1,015Nm and a 0-60mph time of 3.1 seconds, you already know this car will thoroughly rearrange your corporate priorities.

But those figures don’t fully prepare you for the real-world sensation. The acceleration is so immediate that it makes you grateful for the engineering of the headrests. It doesn’t lack manners, but the Polestar 5 Performance will absolutely hijack the road with the silent, shocking efficiency of a corporate restructuring. 

My colleague discovered this quite amusingly. At one point, when it was my mischievous co-driver’s turn in the hot seat, he deliberately stamped on the accelerator just as I was lifting a peach-flavoured can of water towards my lips. None of it made it into my mouth. Quite a lot went over my face, T-shirt and coat.

Naturally, revenge was required. Later, I planted my size-11 firmly on the go pedal while his reading glasses were perched on top of his head. The burst of speed promptly pushed them behind his neck. Payback, in electric form.  

Is it possible the Performance version has more muscle than the average commute requires? Maybe.

Does it offer a high return on investment in terms of pure, unadulterated, wicked entertainment? No question.

Built for London

For a car expected to navigate London’s chaotic traffic at least some of the time, being largely engineered in the UK means the Polestar 5 also speaks the language of potholes and speed humps.

The Dual Motor has sophisticated BWI passive dampers and internal rebound coil springs, and, as mentioned earlier, the Performance gets MagneRide adaptive dampers. This advanced suspension system can read the road up to 1,000 times a second and react within three milliseconds. The result is excellent body motion control and an optimal response at all speeds.

Braking is handled by Brembo four-piston callipers in combination with lightweight 400mm two-piece discs, while Michelin tyres, designed for the Polestar 5’s chosen wheel combinations ranging from 20 to 22 inches, complete the package.

Galvin reiterates the car has been engineered with British roads specifically in mind.

“It’s been developed here,” he says. “So it handles great.”

Having personally driven the 5 in both forms, I can confirm the engineering hasn’t been squandered on a vehicle designed merely for posing outside a London office.

That said, the grand tourer does posing brilliantly.

Business Lounge on Wheels

The Polestar 5 has another side to its character that could prove particularly significant in London.

Its design delivers a spacious rear seating area by repositioning the header structure behind the passengers’ heads and using a digital rear-view mirror with a virtual rear window, similar to the Polestar 4. 

The back seats can cool, heat, individually recline and massage – and rear passengers can control the four-zone climate system. A nifty ‘foot garage’ within the battery structure also creates extra foot space behind the front chairs, meaning occupants in the back have a more natural seating position. 

But wait, there’s more. The 5 is primarily a four-seater, although if you lift the central armrest, the 2+2 car effectively becomes a five-seater. The Polestar also has 365 litres of rear boot space, while the 62-litre front luggage area is handy for a small bag and charging cable.

The cabin itself is minimalist, with natural-fibre materials, recycled textiles and a massive panoramic glass roof measuring over two metres long.

Up front, the Recaro-developed seats marry a low driving position with decent bolstering – although, as alluded to before, even more cushioning wouldn’t go amiss. They come finished in Charcoal MicroTech, or optional Bridge of Weir Nappa leather in Zinc or Charcoal. 

Between the front seats is a low centre console with a lockable storage compartment, topped with a rotary audio controller for the 14.5-inch portrait touchscreen. The unit runs Polestar’s Android Automotive operating system with Google built in, alongside a nine-inch digital instrument screen and slightly bigger head-up display.

Audio comes via the Polestar High-Performance Audio system with 10 speakers, or you can up the ante with 21 speakers courtesy of Bowers & Wilkins, with 1,680 watts of power. The latter’s fidelity is so clean, you can almost hear the recording engineer sipping his brew.

In other words, the Polestar 5 won’t make you regret your life choices during a two-hour traffic jam on the M11.

From London to Heathrow

London isn’t short on power and might, and as you’ll know by now, nor is this new grand tourer. But if you’re in business in the City, the only number that might truly dictate your sanity is your electric car’s range. 

Therefore, you’ll be pleased to read that the Polestar 5 Dual Motor has an official maximum range of 416 miles on a single charge, while the Performance version offers up to 351 miles.

An 800V electrical architecture enables the Polestar flagship to charge at up to 350kW on an appropriate DC charger. A 10-80% battery refill can take just 22 minutes, and an external indicator on the car’s C-pillar gives a first-glance indication of the 5’s state of charge.

Galvin is relaxed and reassuring about any anxiety over electric range.

“I do 20,000 miles a year, and I can count them on one hand, the number of times I do 300 miles in a day.”

His point is straightforward. For most trips, a 350-plus-mile electric vehicle already offers more than many people need.

So, if your working life revolves around London, Heathrow Airport, and the odd long motorway journey, the Polestar 5’s mix of range and rapid charging is especially relevant.

Prestige and Presence

There is also the image element. I mean, let’s be honest, while standard cars handle your commute, expensive vehicles manage your reputation. Because, in certain parts of London, the whip outside the office can say almost as much as the person inside it. 

Consequently, design matters – and the Polestar 5 certainly has presence.

“I drove it around central London last week,” Galvin tells me.

“If you want to get noticed, this is a car for you.”

He says that while travelling through Hammersmith and Wandsworth, people absorbed in their phones suddenly looked up as the Polestar passed.

“They’d look up and do a double take.”

I know what he means. From every angle, the Polestar 5 looks big-ticket, prestigious and utterly modern. It has the visual presence of a car whose driver has made it in life.

A New Choice

The Polestar 5 Dual Motor Launch edition starts at £89,500, and the Performance Launch edition at £104,900.

That puts the electric grand tourer solidly into the premium automotive arena, and that’s exactly where Polestar wants it.

The company is chasing consumers who’ve already experienced the usual suspects and want something that feels fresher, rarer and more distinctive.

As Galvin puts it, the potential customer may already have had a Taycan or an Audi RS e-tron GT and be pondering what comes next.

“Up until now, there wasn’t really an alternative,” he says. “And now there is the Polestar 5”.

So, the 5 gives London’s top executives a clear advantage. It lets them drive a car that radiates wealth while steering clear of their contemporaries’ vanilla choices.

And if your glasses end up behind your neck or you wind up smelling of peaches, that’s merely the price of progress.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent.
